Breaking: Not upgrading to iPhone 18 Pro or Duo? Here’s what’s coming in 2027

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner.
  • 2027 is going to be a relatively substantial iPhone release year for Apple.
  • For the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner. If for whatever reason you’re considering skipping out on this year’s iPhones, here’s what you have to look forward to next year.

2027 is going to be a relatively substantial iPhone release year for Apple. First, the tech giant will be continuing the iPhone 18 lineup after it introduced a split release schedule. Then, in the fall, the company will debut a upcoming round of flagships in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. Here’s what to expect.

For the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring. Upgrades for the iPhone 18 aren’t quite clear, though more RAM is one of the key rumors. Thermal upgrades will likely happen as well, as well as the fresh Apple C2 modem.

It’s possible Apple will update the design to fall more in line with the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro, though we don’t yet know.

This phone will of course equip the A20 chip, and it’ll probably start at the same $899 price point that iPhone 17 currently sits at – after it was increased from $799 in September.

This phone will most likely just end up being a chip bump from the A19 to A20 chip, and debut in the Spring alongside the iPhone 18. Earlier this year, reports indicated that Apple would share many components between the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, though it isn’t quite clear what that could mean for the devices.

In a recent development, out of all of the spring iPhone releases, this one is the one to look forward to. After receiving a lukewarm reception with the initial iPhone Air model, Apple went back to the drawing board and decided to modify the design to fit an ultrawide camera into the device.

Personally, I don’t think an ultrawide camera is too crucial – though many people will see one camera on the back of the phone and immediately assume it’s less premium, so it’ll probably end up being an important upgrade for the sake of sales. Plus, ultrawide photos can be fun at times.

It has been revealed that it should also have a larger battery, reportedly as large as 3500mAh. That’s a roughly 10% improvement from the original iPhone Air. iPhone Air 2 will likely also jump from Apples C1X modem to the C2.

In a recent development, for the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, Apple is expected to debut a fully redesigned iPhone to celebrate. It’ll reportedly be much more glassy, feature significantly slimmer bezels, a quad curved display, and ditch the flat edge design of the iPhone 12 and later.

Recent findings suggest that personally, I’m slightly skeptical that this’ll truly be a replacement to the “Pro” phone for thermal reasons, but time will tell. iPhone Duo seemingly has strong thermals while not featuring an aluminum unibody, so my concern might not be relevant. It’ll offer two, larger display sizes: 6.4-inch and 7-inch. This largely comes from the bezel reduction.

I wish they prioritized the Telephoto camera more. I need that (whether it be on an Air or a Duo) way more than an Ultrawide.

If you’re holding out for iPhone 18 Pro, this “iPhone 20” is definitely the phone to wait out for.

Lastly, Apple will release a successor to its just-announced iPhone Duo next fall. Of course, you can expect next-generation Apple Silicon with the A21 Pro chip next year, but there aren’t many other substantial changes expected. Apple may bring proper Face ID to the outer display, an improvement from the recently-announced face unlock, but it’s unclear whether this feature will make the engineering cutoff date.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sierra, the AI agent company co-founded by OpenAI chair Bret Taylor, is raising $1.75B at a $30B valuation, led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed.
  • Recent findings suggest that sierra, the AI customer service tech giant led by Bret Taylor, is raising $1.75B at a $30B valuation, it announced on Monday.
  • The valuation is almost double the $15.8B Sierra was worth in May, when it raised $950M.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sierra, the AI agent company co-founded by OpenAI chair Bret Taylor, is raising $1.75B at a $30B valuation, led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed. That is almost double the $15.8B it was valued at in May, and it says annual recurring revenue has passed $400M.

Recent findings suggest that sierra, the AI customer service tech giant led by Bret Taylor, is raising $1.75B at a $30B valuation, it announced on Monday. Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners are leading the round.

The valuation is almost double the $15.8B Sierra was worth in May, when it raised $950M. All of its previous lead investors, including Benchmark, Sequoia and Tiger Global, are investing again.

Sierra builds AI agents that answer customers’ calls and messages for large companies. It indicates its annual recurring revenue passed $400M in October, just over two and a half years after launch. Almost half of the Fortune 50 are customers, it says.

Sierra charges for outcomes, such as a resolved problem or a paid insurance claim, rather than per seat or per token, and Zendesk is moving the same way. Insurer Guardian recently handed it 1 million dental calls a year, and its agents can now take card payments through Stripe.

Taylor, who also chairs OpenAI’s board, co-founded Sierra with former Google executive Clay Bavor. In a blog post, the pair addressed fears of an AI bubble.

“We’re seeing some of the oldest, most regulated companies in the world deploy AI the fastest,” they wrote. They pointed to last week’s record Anthropic IPO as a sign of how fast AI is moving.

Competition in AI customer service is heating up. In June, Salesforce agreed to buy support-AI firm Fin for $3.6B.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that although Black Friday is still a few days away, the deals are already filtering in. If you're after a upcoming mechanical keyboard — maybe your first, maybe your 10th, or if you're anything like me, maybe your 50th — this is easily the best time of year to get one.

Sources indicate that I'm Pete. I've reviewed dozens of mechanical keyboards, tested and owned dozens more, and edited hundreds of keyboard reviews from my team. At the risk of sounding my own horn, I'm a keyboard expert. So I follow pricing throughout the year.

I've rounded up some of my favorite early Black Friday keyboard deals here. My top pick is the Keychron C2 Pro 8K, now just $48 at Amazon — it offers nearly unparalleled value for money. There are plenty more deals where that came from, though. All these boards have been tested personally by me or my team, and they all scored high — to do that, by definition, they had to be excellent to type on.

Cute and compact, we gave the Logitech Pebble Keys 2 our Recommended badge and 4 coveted stars in our review. Circular keycaps might not be for everyone, but this will still certainly be an upgrade over a crappy work keyboard or tired laptop keyboard.

Recent findings suggest that this keyboard practically defines value for money. We tested the 80% variant, the Keychron C1 Pro 8K, which is essentially the same board without a num pad. It offers excellent typing and solid gaming performance, too. And now for under $50.

My first mechanical keyboard was the Keychron K2, so it holds a special place in my heart. This is an excellent starter keyboard for a first time mechanical user. This variant isn't hot-swappable like the C2 Pro above, so the C2 is better if you want to customize your board. However, if you're after a more compact 75% layout, I heartily recommend the K2.

Recent findings suggest that I awarded this board a full five star score in my Keychron V6 review. If typing is your main priority and you don't need the gaming features of the C2 Pro, the V6 is incredible value for money. It's also designed to be a starting point for custom builds, as you can fully take it apart, so great for newcomers to the custom scene — you can experiment with modding but not drop too much cash.

According to recent reports, I loved this board in my Lofree Flow Lite review. In typical Lofree style, it's beautiful to behold, oozing minimalist charm. Thanks to Lofree's long-running partnership with switch manufacturer Kailh, you're also getting some of the best switches on the market for typing. Hardcore typists who need a portable, low-profile deck: this one's for you.

Fancy adding some fun to your desk? The Gravastar Mercury K1, which we gave four stars, never fails to turn heads. While I didn't review it personally (our writer Nikita did), I used this as my main gaming keyboard for several months at home. It types and sounds absolutely gorgeous. (macOS users be warned, this deck only really works properly on Windows or Linux.).

Industry observers note that our staff writer Nikita (the only person on our team to have reviewed more keyboards than me!) gave the Epomaker Glyph our Editor's Choice badge in her review. Despite having the pick of literally any keyboard she could choose, she still uses this as her daily work driver. So yeah, it's awesome. Looks great, sounds epic, types even better.

Alright, so this one isn't actually a mechanical board. It's magnetic. However, the K2 HE is still an absolute weapon for typing — adjustable actuation lets you dial in your switch behavior to optimize type speeds. And naturally, as a Hall Effect deck, it's a total demon for gaming too.

I tested the NuPhy Air75 V3, this board's little sibling, and absolutely loved it. If you're after a low-profile board with drop-dead gorgeous looks, captivating sound and effortless typing, here it is.

Still probably the best sounding keyboard we've ever tested, I spent several weeks using the Rainy 75 Pro as my daily driver at work. The creamy raindrop-esque clack is utterly addictive, and this board is a perfect candidate for modding too.

Arguably rather overpriced at MSRP, the Lofree DOT still captured my heart when I reviewed it. Lofree's styling is second to none, and the DOT's circular keycaps give you that retro type-writer-esque experience. It's still expensive at this sale price, but a hell of a lot more palatable than the list price, and I'd definitely say worth it.

  • It has been revealed that in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield.
  • Sources indicate that in the first half, Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

It has been revealed that in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar indicates how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

Sources indicate that in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session reveals how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

Jensen Huang at the White House AI Summit at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, D.C., 23 July 2025.

It has been revealed that jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s chief executive on Monday drew cheers from the investors who campaigned for it. Its critics were scornful. Many of them reacted on X within minutes of the board’s decision.

Business Insider gathered the posts, along with comments from analysts and critics who wrote elsewhere.

Elon Musk had signed the letter calling for Huang’s reinstatement and compared his exit to dropping Michael Jordan. On Monday he replied to Nvidia’s announcement.

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 23, 2026.

This month Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital co-wrote a letter asking the board to bring Huang back, with Atreides’ Gavin Baker. He posted a screenshot of the CNBC news with one word, “Unanimous”, and an American flag.

Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick had promised to turn up at Nvidia’s headquarters with a “wafer-encrusted megaphone” to call for a walkout. On Monday he posted a picture of the megaphone. He wrote that he would save it for another day.

All-In co-host Jason Calacanis posted an edited picture of Huang as Jesus, and wrote: “GPU Jesus has risen!”.

Industry observers note that going on @MSNOWNews with @SRuhle shortly to chop it up! https://t.co/yZKSpzFzxq.

— @jason (@Jason) November 23, 2026.

According to recent reports, openAI’s Sam Altman, whose own board fired and rehired him in 2023, had declined to say whether Huang should return. On Monday he wrote one word: “Jensen!”.

— Sam Altman (@sama) November 23, 2026.

Former Goldman Sachs chief executive Lloyd Blankfein took aim at the board.

According to recent reports, guess you can come back from the graveyard if you’re really, really, really indispensable. The NVDA board will not have that opportunity.

— Lloyd Blankfein (@lloydblankfein) November 23, 2026.

Katie Miller, the former DOGE lead, said Huang had done “more than an Altman” and the “same as a Scaramucci”. Anthony Scaramucci lasted 10 days as White House communications director.

Industry observers note that sequoia partner Shaun Maguire wrote that markets were “ripping” on the news. US stocks rose on Monday after the Dow, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq ended Friday in correction territory, CNBC reported. The S&P 500 fell more than 9% from Huang’s exit on 12 November to Friday.

Industry observers note that nvidia’s shares jumped 33%, putting it on course to add $900bn in market value, Reuters reported. CoreWeave and Nebius, cloud companies Nvidia has invested in, rose nearly 25%.

“It tells us to some extent that Jensen Huang was too substantial to be fired,” Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, told Reuters.

#97299. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3541 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Recent findings suggest that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

According to recent reports, the screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics tech giant. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

Recent findings suggest that for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

Industry observers note that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Sources indicate that yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

Sources indicate that the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

Industry observers note that if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

In a recent development, sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team revealed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

Recent findings suggest that I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

Sources indicate that this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga indicates. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Sources indicate that dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Fresh York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

According to recent reports, in the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics tech giant XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

In a recent development, “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Recent findings suggest that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

According to recent reports, after preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

In a recent development, noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga claims.

In a recent development, still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

According to recent reports, but sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” states neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

It has been revealed that but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

Industry observers note that and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu indicates.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” states neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Recent findings suggest that telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra notes, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

In a recent development, “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

Sources indicate that in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Industry observers note that neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell indicates. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

Sources indicate that the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as swiftly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell states. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy revealed US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

In a recent development, sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

Industry observers note that the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this newly introduced technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

It has been revealed that these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person tech giant into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print concern as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”.

The analyst also noted completion of a 14-mile Hugh Brinson lateral in Abilene, Texas, and final stages of talks for an additional 250 mmcfd of Oklahoma power plant demand.

Tonet ranks No. 922 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 9%. See Energy Transfer Financials on TipRanks.

Industry observers note that the 5-star analyst noted that while PR stock has outperformed its peers so far in 2026, he sees further upside. Smith noted that the derating of weaker California peers PG&E (PCG) and Edison International (EIX) is weighing on the sum-of-the-parts (SOTP) valuation but is becoming less relevant given their materially higher fire risk compared to Sempra Energy.

Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott has called Jensen Huang to a public hearing at 10am on Thursday, 3 December, according to a notice. The hearing will come less than two weeks after Nvidia’s board reinstated him as chief executive, Politico reported.

Huang had agreed to testify before his return. A spokesperson for Huang declined to comment on whether his intends have changed, Politico’s Jasper Goodman reported.

Lawmakers from both parties criticised the board’s decision on Monday. Several said it made it more urgent to pass tighter controls on chip exports to China.

It has been revealed that nvidia’s board said in its announcement that it relied on input from senior levels of the US government. On that basis, it said Huang’s return poses no national security risk. Senator John Cornyn of Texas asked what that was based on.

— Senator John Cornyn (@JohnCornyn) November 23, 2026.

Brian Mast, who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called the reports about Huang “extremely concerning” on X. In a video posted minutes after the announcement, he remarked Huang still owes Congress answers under oath. A committee spokesperson told Politico the committee still expects Huang’s closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December to go ahead.

Sources indicate that “The American people deserve answers on Mr. Huang’s relationship with this potential Chinese intelligence asset,” Mast said.

As Chairman of the @HouseForeignGOP, export controls on our most advanced AI chips has been a top priority. The reports of Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a Chinese intelligence asset and the smuggling of our most advanced technology to China is extremely concerning.

The American people deserve answers.

— Rep. Brian Mast (@RepBrianMast) November 23, 2026.

Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska remarked Nvidia should have moved on without Huang, Reuters reported.

“Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy,” Bacon noted.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said in a statement that the administration’s role in Huang’s return showed Congress must act.

“Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Schumer remarked.

Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi called the decision “outrageous” on X. He stated Trump’s assurances could not be taken at face value, citing a $25m donation from Nvidia to Trump’s ballroom. Huang must testify at a full public hearing, he wrote.

Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang is outrageous. We still don’t know what information Chinese intelligence may have obtained from him, and neither the government nor Nvidia’s own board has completed its investigation.

Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom.

Huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him. https://t.co/9d2XnHNxtV.

— Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi (@CongressmanRaja) November 23, 2026.

It has been revealed that representative Debbie Dingell called the decision irresponsible, as Congress has not yet heard from Huang. Representative Richard Neal remarked the board’s reference to “input from senior levels” was one of many reasons Congress needs answers, Reuters reported. Senator Elizabeth Warren had already called the move “reckless”.

Industry observers note that senator Ruben Gallego went further. He wrote on X that Trump was selling out national security to keep the stock market high.

The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some fucking donation to his ballroom.

— Ruben Gallego (@RubenGallego) November 23, 2026.

Huang’s return is likely to affect his legal representation before Congress, Semafor reported. The administration might also push back on the oversight aims, it stated.

Leaders in both parties are leaning towards using the coming defence bill to close gaps in chip export policy, Semafor reported. Mast is among those pushing to attach export control bills to the National Defense Authorization Act, according to Politico.

Trump told CNBC on Monday that he did not think the board would have brought Huang back without him. The White House did not respond to Semafor’s request for comment.

According to recent reports, cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

Sources indicate that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

Sources indicate that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

Type: Memory foam and latexBest for: Combination sleepersSizes: standard and high loftTrial: 45 nightsWarranty: 1-yearPrice: $165 at Saatva.

As the name suggests, the Graphite Memory Foam Pillow is made with mostly memory foam with a little bit of shredded natural latex thrown into the mix. It has a different design to any of the best pillows I've tested before — a thin shredded latex core, sandwiched by two slabs of graphite-infused memory foam for, apparently, improved breathability (spoiler: this was not my experience).

It has been revealed that I tested a queen-size Graphite Memory Foam Pillow in standard loft, but it's also available in a high loft. The surface is on the firmer side and, thanks to its memory foam construction, offers a little contouring. Although I prefer a plusher feel, the surface isn’t what makes this pillow uncomfortable. It was how the bottom edge of the pillow seemed to squish flat, causing my neck to sit at an unnatural angle, or my head to slide off — depending on which position I was sleeping in.

Another big drawback had to do with the temperature regulation. Despite testing during November when my house was cool at night, I woke up to warm spots on the pillow.

If you've read enough and want a quick signpost to a more comfortable alternative, check out my review of the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow (I rated it 4.5/5).But if you're still wondering if the Saatva Graphite Memory Foam pillow could be the right fit for you, strap yourself in for my full review below.

Saatva is a premium mattress brand, and that’s reflected in the price of their pillows too. The Graphite Memory Foam Pillow has an MSRP price of $165 for a standard loft, queen size pillow. Bedding and accessories aren't included in the current Saatva Black Friday sale. However, you do stand to save $40 when you buy as part of a Sateen Sheet Set bundle.

In my opinion, the $165 price tag is steep, especially considering how much of the pillow is comprised of memory foam and there are no certifications for the organic cotton cover or the natural latex.

The Saatva Graphite Memory Foam Pillow is available in two different lofts and costs $165. In a recent development, like many of the best pillows we've tested, there’s a lot more going on with the design of this pillow than appears from the outside. It’s sold in a standard (4-5" tall) or high loft (6-7" tall), with the high loft more suitable to broader bodies.

Sources indicate that the pillow effectively has three main layers, starting with a removeable knit cotton cover. Below the cotton cover is an 'inner pillow.' Two medium-thick blocks of memory foam infused with graphite are placed on the front and the back sides of the inner pillow. Memory foam is not a breathable foam, so graphite is used to promote a cool night’s sleep.

In a recent development, between the memory foam blocks is a bag that contains shredded natural latex and memory foam. It’s quite thin and can be removed entirely from the inner pillow if need be. However, you can’t open that core to add or remove the shredded foams.

Lastly, the memory foam has a CertiPUR-US certification. Although Saatva say the cover is made with organic cotton and they include natural latex in the pillow, no other certifications are provided that verify this.

After one week of testing, here’s what I can tell you about the Saatva Graphite Memory Foam Pillow’s comfort and temperature regulation.

In a recent development, the Saatva Graphite Memory Foam Pillow arrived in a plastic bag within a cardboard box. It was already fully expanded, so I was able to take it out of the bag and sleep on it right away. Unfortunately, I noticed off gassing from this pillow right away, and even more so when I slept on the pillow. As someone with a sensitive nose, I tried to sleep on my back, so I wouldn’t have to smell the pillow.

Sources indicate that A week before I tested Saatva’s Graphite Memory Foam Pillow, I tested the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow. I’m not a huge fan of memory foam but I found the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow to be extremely comfortable. Unfortunately, I couldn’t say the same of the Saatva Graphite Memory Foam Pillow.

I ordered it in the standard loft size which, according to its dimensions, should have been the perfect size to allow me to sleep on my back, stomach, and side. However, it didn’t matter which way I slept, I couldn’t find any position that was particularly comfortable. And there is a single reason why.

In a recent development, when I laid my head down, it didn’t sink into the pillow very much. There was some slight contouring. But at the same time, the bottom length of the pillow (near my shoulders), flattened down creating a significant angle that offered no support to my neck or shoulders. I tried to move the inner shredded latex and memory foam core to prevent this flattening, but nothing seemed to work.

Recent findings suggest that if I slept on my stomach, my head would slide off the pillow. On my side or my back? My neck would feel strained. Because the bottom had flattened out, my neck was not being held up and thus would dip down at an odd angle. If I was lying on my back, my head would be pushed forward more – which wasn’t comfortable. On my side, I was having to hold my head in place or put my hand under the bottom of the pillow to sort of fluff it up.

All in all, I did not sleep well on this pillow during testing.

Bedding brands have long claimed that infusing graphite into memory foam can offer significant cooling properties. I haven’t ever experienced such a thing, not with Saatva’s Graphite Memory Foam Topper and not with this Graphite Memory Foam Pillow.

I didn’t wake up hot and sweaty when sleeping on this pillow. However, I would wake up and notice warm spots around my head. This was odd considering I tested the pillow in November when my home dropped to the 60s at night. I used a breathable Quince linen pillowcase during this time, too.

Industry observers note that I think the lack of breathability in this pillow has a lot to do with the design, in particular, those two blocks of memory foam on the front and back of the pillow. Memory foam doesn’t allow for much air to flow through and dissipate heat.

Most pillows should be replaced after two years. However, if you notice the loft breaking down quicker or your pillow having trouble bouncing back if you fold it in half, you should replace it as soon as possible.

I only slept on the Graphite Memory Foam Pillow for one week, and in that time, I haven’t noticed any signs of sagging or breakdown. Saatva include high-quality, premium materials in their products and estimates longer lifespans for their bedding, so I’m sure you don’t have to worry about this pillow breaking down promptly. That stated, the one-year warranty is on the low end of warranties for premium pillow brands.

The cotton cover of the Graphite Memory Foam Pillow is removeable and can be thrown in the wash. Machine wash it on cold with a delicate cycle then tumble dry the cover on low or hang it to dry.

It has been revealed that remember, to wash the cover on occasion as it can absorb sweat stains, facial cream, or even saliva. This will help extend the lifespan of your pillow. If you notice that anything has bled through to the inner pillow, you can spot clean it as needed.

Recent findings suggest that usually when I test a pillow, there’s at least one type of sleeper I can suggest the pillow to – but that’s not the case with the Saatva Graphite Memory Foam Pillow. Not only does it sleep warm at night, but the design of the pillow resulted in a variety of issues for my neck or head no matter if I was sleeping on my side, stomach, or back.

It has been revealed that the materials aren’t certified organic or completely non-toxic and you can only wash the cover. At least you get the chance to order it in standard or high loft. Considering all the flaws, the price doesn’t feel worth it, even with a 45-night trial with free returns.

I hate to say this about a Saatva product, but they have plenty of others like the Saatva Down Alternative Pillow or the Cloud Memory Foam Pillow that are far more comfortable and/or worth their price.

It has been revealed that google Search’s AI Mode can now use your Google Wallet to give more personal answers, the company confirmed on Monday. Drive and the Gemini app will follow in the coming weeks. It is the latest step in Google’s AI overhaul of Search, unveiled at I/O in May.

The opt-in connections are part of Personal Intelligence, which already lets AI Mode draw on Gmail, Calendar and Photos. With Wallet linked, AI Mode can suggest ways to trim spending and make the most of cash-back and reward points on cards stored in Wallet. Google says the link is read-only, so AI Mode cannot move, manage or invest money.

Sources indicate that with Drive connected, AI Mode can use documents, spreadsheets and PDFs, for example to draw up a strategy for tax season. Linking the Gemini app will let ideas explored in one carry over to the other.

Industry observers note that google rolled out the same Wallet link in Gemini for US users ten days ago, and OpenAI has let some ChatGPT users link bank accounts since May. Users can switch each app on or off under Connected Apps in Search Personalization, and a new icon will show what personal context a response used.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for every field, circuits for the Hamiltonian cycle polynomial, and for the permanent outside characteristic 2, need more than m^(c (log m)^(1/3)) gates for all large m. The same holds for approximating circuits. So VP is a proper subset of VNP, and VNP is not contained in the closure of VP. This does not settle P vs NP.

Sources indicate that the result was discovered by an internal research Claude model. This folder holds the paper and its Lean 4 formalization. Both were written by AI models, and no human mathematician has checked the proof.

Research artifact. Not maintained and not accepting contributions.

It has been revealed that paper.pdf: VP ≠ VNP over every field, by Claude (Anthropic). The full proof is its appendix.

Industry observers note that 1. Read the statement. Statement.lean states all of the above and imports only Mathlib. Lean checks the proofs, but no machine checks that this file states what is claimed. Appendix Q of paper.pdf lists the Lean counterparts of the numbered statements (Table 3) and says where they differ.

Sources indicate that 2. Check the proofs. With elan installed, in this folder:.

The build prints sorry warnings from Challenge.lean only, which states the theorems without proofs for the fuller check. The last command should name no axiom other than propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

The fuller check is the one this repository's CI runs, bash ../.github/scripts/comparator-check.sh (Linux): Comparator compares the statements with Challenge.lean and re-checks the proofs with a second, independently written kernel, nanoda.

Five recent tech outages were not due to AI; the next round will be

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five major tech outages in quick succession earlier this month led to speculation that they were connected, with some inevitably believing them to be AI-related.
  • That wasn’t the case, but the US Director of National Intelligence is one of a number of experts warning that we should expect AI-powered outages in the near future ….
  • According to recent reports, earlier this month saw five tech outages, one after the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five major tech outages in quick succession earlier this month led to speculation that they were connected, with some inevitably believing them to be AI-related.

That wasn’t the case, but the US Director of National Intelligence is one of a number of experts warning that we should expect AI-powered outages in the near future ….

According to recent reports, earlier this month saw five tech outages, one after the other. A widespread Microsoft 365 outage occurred when two unrelated issues coincided. The next day saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. A few days later, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Many Apple services went offline later the same week, with retail stores also affected. Finally, United Airlines had its own widespread IT outage that grounded a significant number of flights.

Each had their own unrelated causes, with the White House stating that rumors of an AI-facilitated systemic attack by a hostile state were false.

Recent findings suggest that however, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has warned that we should expect future tech outages as a result of attacks facilitated by AI-discovered vulnerabilities. CNBC reports him issuing the warning on CNN’s State of the Union.

The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.

You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot.

We already saw an example of this last month when a vulnerability discovered in PHP saw a significant number of websites being taken offline.

Microsoft President Brad Smith says it isn’t just a question of bad actors exploiting vulnerabilities discovered by AI, but companies rushing to patch these may inadvertently cause systems to fail, as Newsweek reports.

What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code, and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems.

Especially when you have older infrastructure, especially when you’re trying to patch at such a pace, especially when you have to go so fast that you can’t take as much time to test what you’re changing in the code, you do increase the risk of something going wrong.

Major IT failures look set to be a routine event in the coming weeks and months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most dramatic shifts in the AI landscape is the emergence of intelligent agents that can use iPhone and Mac apps in order to carry out tasks on our behalf.

Recent findings suggest that we can already use third-party chatbots in this way, and we know Apple is working hard to turn Siri AI into an agent. However, before the company even gets the chance, banks are already blocking them, and this may be just the start ….

The science fiction promise of AI has always been to be able to tell a computer what we want done and have the task carried out for us automatically. That’s starting to turn into a reality with the emergence of AI agents.

We’ve already seen Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, and Muse gain agent capabilities, and Apple is expected to bring these to Siri AI at some point next year.

It has been revealed that earlier this month, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said that the company ultimately wants to go in this direction and may add these abilities next year. CEO John Ternus has reportedly been pushing Craig Federighi for faster software development, with specific mention of “moving beyond necessary improvements to Siri,” which seems likely to mean agentic capabilities.

Last week also saw a since-deleted Apple job listing detailing looks for autonomous AI agents.

It has been revealed that we’ve already seen some of the ways in which this can go wrong, and we recently outlined three significant risks. Wired reports that banks are now responding to these by either blocking AI agents or warning customers that using them can be dangerous.

Wells Fargo even goes as far as using capitals in its latest terms, stating that it will not be responsible for the consequences.

Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK.

We can likely expect similar pushback in sectors like online shopping as companies fear high returns costs and other consequences from mistakes by AI agents.

Recent findings suggest that personally, I don’t give any AI agents access to any of my banking or other financial services, considering the risks to be too high. I don’t see my position changing any time soon.

What’s your take? Would you trust an AI agent with access to your bank accounts? If not, would Apple launching agentic capabilities for Siri AI change your view? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

It has been revealed that I didn’t know what to expect from this 1937 video explanation of how wire photos were transmitted to newspapers, but a double stunt sequence featuring an airplane and a death-defying photographer was not anywhere on my bingo card. This starts kinda slow but it picks up once they get into the completely fascinating explanation of how they sent photographs across the country using ordinary telephone lines. The whole setup was portable and they just hacked into a wire on a telephone pole, asked the operator to clear the line, and sent a photo scan via an analog modem. Ingenious!

The Wikipedia page about wire photos is worth a read — French designers argued that the technology was responsible for an early form of fast fashion.

Sources indicate that sort by: thread — thread . latest . faves.

Sources indicate that hi, journalist here, this wild technology was still in use into the early 90s at least. I remember working at a little paper in South Carolina when AP rolled out an early way to see photos on a computer screen instead of waiting for the wacky old spinning drum machines to spit out prints, one by one, that you'd physically thumb through. It felt like magic. But truth be told, the spinning drum thing was also magic.

You can read more about wire photos on Tedium: Pushing Photos Through Wires.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia has declared that disgraced CEO Jensen Huang has been reinstated to the role, effective immediately. The firm’s share price jumped more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also making significant gains.

It said that the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstatement despite its recent statement that it had no intention of doing so ….

It has been revealed that huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy became the main headline news in the tech press after coming to light at the end of last month. The Upcoming York Times broke the story on October 29, citing it then as “a close relationship.” Nvidia initially denied that the relationship was anything out of the ordinary.

That changed on November 8 when Huang publicly admitted to the affair. Nvidia’s shares dropped 5%, and the firm’s board of directors opened an independent investigation. Further details emerged over the following days. Things got even worse when the same paper reported that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

That led to Huang being fired resigning on November 12.

He won’t make that mistake again!

According to recent reports, despite putting the company at enormous risk and initially lying to its board of directors, there were calls in some quarters for Huang to be reinstated. He responded by saying that he would be “honored” to return if asked to do so.

The board of directors, however, said that it had no intention of inviting him back.

Nvidia’s chair Harvey Jones remarked: “The board does not intend to reinstate him.”.

That changed today, with the tech giant making the announcement in a press release.

Sources indicate that nvidia today confirmed that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

In a recent development, “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” remarked Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”.

It has been revealed that as previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A global coalition of more than 150 child safety groups and experts has asked Amazon and eBay to stop selling toys with built-in AI chatbots.
  • Recent findings suggest that the campaign is led by the nonprofit Fairplay, joined by groups such as Zero to Three and Jonathan Haidt’s Anxious Generation Movement, with signatories from every continent except Antarctica.
  • The groups want the toys pulled “this holiday season and until they are proven safe.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A global coalition of more than 150 child safety groups and experts has asked Amazon and eBay to stop selling toys with built-in AI chatbots. The request came in an open letter sent on Monday to Amazon CEO Andy Jassy and eBay CEO Jamie Iannone.

Recent findings suggest that the campaign is led by the nonprofit Fairplay, joined by groups such as Zero to Three and Jonathan Haidt’s Anxious Generation Movement, with signatories from every continent except Antarctica. The letter notes that over 50 AI toys were recently found on sale on Amazon in the US.

The groups want the toys pulled “this holiday season and until they are proven safe.”.

It has been revealed that their worries will sound familiar to anyone who followed this year’s AI toy scares. The toys can produce sexual or otherwise inappropriate responses, their microphones raise privacy risks in the playroom, and none of it has passed independent safety testing.

The letter argues the two marketplaces already remove unsafe products, so suspending the listings is well within their power. Beyond that, it asks the companies to warn customers of the dangers. Moreover, the campaigners want a public answer before Christmas, so they can take their case to governments and parents.

Amazon has already moved a little, and the firm mentioned it removed some AI toys that NBC News and a consumer group had recently tested.

Pressure is coming from several directions at once, as a group of parliamentarians wrote to the two companies earlier this month with the same demand. Some retailers and toy makers have also started pulling AI toys of their own accord.

The campaign also marks an escalation, as last year, Fairplay and its allies simply told parents not to buy the toys; this year, they are going after the shelves themselves.

#97275. Will Siri AI threaten Apple’s environmental target, given Google and Meta admissions?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (989 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Will Siri AI threaten Apple’s environmental target, given Google and Meta admissions?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials.
  • All of this could potentially be put at risk by the manufacturer’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services ….
  • Industry observers note that apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials. It has led the way with its use of renewable energy, made significant strides with carbon-neutral production, and removed plastic from all its packaging.

All of this could potentially be put at risk by the manufacturer’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services ….

Industry observers note that apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect. For example, when it claimed that the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 were carbon neutral back in 2023, that claim was described as “bogus,” with the EU banning Apple from repeating it. The organization has also been criticized for pushing a relentless annual iPhone cycle, encouraging frequent upgrades.

Overall, however, Apple has first-rate credentials when it comes to the environment. It was way back in 2018 when the organization hit its goal of running its own operations off 100% renewable energy. This includes all Apple facilities, from Apple Park through data centers to its worldwide retail store network.

I said at the time that using more environmentally friendly packaging should be the company’s next priority, and it has indeed made great progress with this over the years, succeeding in removing all plastic packaging earlier this year.

It has been revealed that after its own operations, Apple set about trying to tackle the power usage of its manufacturing partners. Back in 2020, the company set a goal of having its entire supply chain be carbon neutral by 2030. Just four years later, Apple said it was 95% of the way there.

The company also helps fund and support a wide range of environmental initiatives around the world. Just a few examples include conservation in China’s national parks, environmental protection and carbon removal in Australia and Fresh Zealand, and helping to fund the build-out of renewable energy capacity in India.

Potentially, however, the vast energy demands of the data centers powering AI services could put its 2030 goal at risk. Other tech giants have already admitted that it may lead them to fail to hit their own renewable energy promises.

Back in 2024, for example, Google CEO Sundar Pichai stated that the AI boom was “challenging” to the tech giant’s 2030 carbon-free goal. CNET reports that Meta is now also admitting that it may fail to hit the same target.

Meta’s data center and sustainability chiefs wrote that the tech giant is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets.” In an emailed statement to CNET, a Meta spokesperson added, “We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline.”.

Notably, a lot of Siri’s most advanced AI capabilities are currently powered by Google’s Gemini models.

At the same 2024 event where Google expressed doubts, Apple reiterated its commitment to its 2030 target. Then-CEO Tim Cook repeated this assurance later the same year, although admitted it would be challenging.

More challenges, yes. But are we coming off the goal? No, definitely not. With more data centers, you use more renewable energy, and we’ve built that muscle now […] I feel very good about 2030.

In the manufacturer’s most recent environmental progress report, it remarked that it was was still using 100% renewable energy despite using over 2.5 billion kWh of electricity to power its data centers.

We’re proud that 100 percent of that electricity came from renewable sources including solar, wind, and low-impact hydropower. To cover our needs, we build our own renewable power projects and work with utilities to purchase clean energy from locally obtained resources. We’re staying at 100 percent even as Apple’s data center capacity continues to grow.

The same report noted the tech giant had achieved zero water use for cooling at its latest data centers.

At our three newest data centers, we use high-efficiency air-cooled chillers instead of water-cooled systems, resulting in zero water use for cooling.

Recent findings suggest that however, the greatest challenge for Apple lies ahead. The reason that Google and Meta are now backtracking on their promises is that both companies now have massive AI capabilities. As yet, Apple does not.

In a recent development, what happens as Apple expands Siri AI capabilities as usage increases, and as the company moves into agentic AI features? Is it realistic for the company to maintain its 100% track record with vastly greater data center energy usage?

Greenpeace expressed its own doubts earlier this year.

“AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” spokesperson Avex Li says. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the company will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”.

Apple did not respond directly but merely pointed to its past statements and most recent environmental progress report.

I don’t doubt the company’s desire to maintain its track record, but if Apple does join the likes of Google and Meta in becoming a major AI player, sticking to its 2030 timing is going to become increasingly difficult.

Do you think Apple will succeed? Please share your thoughts in the comments.
