iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017.
  • With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch.
  • I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories.

With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the newly introduced GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 ($149, reg. $249) experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios.

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

Industry observers note that as a side note: Apple Watch has more accurate treadmill workout tracking as part of watchOS 27. GymKit remains the gold standard for accurate data, though.

In a recent development, gymKit also avoids two awkward gym habits. You don’t need to hold the treadmill’s metal heart-rate contacts while jogging. You also do not need to wear a Bluetooth heart-rate strap.

AirPods Pro 3 become the heart-rate source (and likely your podcast or music audio source as well). iPhone becomes the workout computer, which you can monitor during your workout. And the treadmill fills in the machine data while providing the surface for walking or running.

Sources indicate that apple has been moving more fitness features onto iPhone for years. iOS first made the Fitness app useful without Apple Watch as Apple Fitness+ leaned into iPhone as an entry point. AirPods Pro 3 pushed that further as the first AirPods with heart-rate tracking, after Apple tested the idea with Powerbeats Pro 2.

It has been revealed that iOS 27 brings those pieces together. GymKit on iPhone shouldn’t replace Apple Watch for people who wear one every day. Instead, it’s a great backup when your Apple Watch is dead, charging, or left at home.

It also gives iPhone and AirPods consumers a taste of the Apple Watch experience, which could attract future Apple Watch customers.

It has been revealed that in testing with iOS 27 beta 1, my Exercise ring didn’t update as I worked out without wearing Apple Watch. But after I put my watch back on, the Exercise ring caught up, and the workout appeared in Fitness with the right data.

My sample 16-minute treadmill walk demonstrated 0.66 miles, 65 active calories, 97 total calories, 32 feet of elevation gain, and a 115 BPM average heart rate, just like if I’d worn an Apple Watch.

Recent findings suggest that I had been getting the impression that gym equipment manufacturers had been abandoning GymKit support - if they ever had done so initially. I even got the impression that the majority of equipment in Apple's own onsite Gym at the Apple Park may not have supported it - at least originally.

In a recent development, does Apple have a webpage listing compatible brands and models? Like they do/did for HomeKit.

What is other people perception? Any rowing machines that support it?

…checks - surprisingly it looks like Peloton do support it on their bikes.

If I tried to use GymKit on iPhone without AirPods, the iPhone disconnected when the workout started because it had no heart-rate source. If I tried to start GymKit from iPhone while wearing Apple Watch, iOS pointed me back to the Workout app on Apple Watch instead, though you can continue without using the watch.

In a recent development, airPods heart-rate permission also matters. You can manage it in Settings under your AirPods settings and privacy options. I had turned it off, mostly as a theoretical battery-saving move, but this test convinced me to turn it back on. AirPods Pro 3 can also work with Apple Watch to provide the best available heart-rate data.

In a recent development, gymKit on iPhone is one of those iOS 27 features that sounds small until it solves a real problem. If Apple Watch is your default workout tracker, it probably stays that way.

But if your watch dies or you forget it at home, iPhone plus AirPods Pro 3 can now log a treadmill workout with real heart-rate data and real treadmill metrics.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Effective immediately, Nvidia’s Board of Directors just voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as President, CEO and board director — just 11 days after he resigned amid an explosive espionage and extramarital affair scandal, and a mere six days after the company insisted it had no intention of bringing him back.
  • It has been revealed that if you blinked over the last two weeks, you might have missed the entire post-Jensen Huang era of Nvidia.
  • So what changed between last Tuesday’s firm “no” and this morning’s unanimous “welcome back”?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Effective immediately, Nvidia’s Board of Directors just voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as President, CEO and board director — just 11 days after he resigned amid an explosive espionage and extramarital affair scandal, and a mere six days after the company insisted it had no intention of bringing him back.

It has been revealed that if you blinked over the last two weeks, you might have missed the entire post-Jensen Huang era of Nvidia. It is the kind of corporate whiplash that makes Sam Altman’s infamous five-day OpenAI ousting look like PTO. To make sense of how the world’s most consequential chipmaker pulled off a full-speed reverse, you have to look at the sheer chaos of the last 25 days.

So what changed between last Tuesday’s firm “no” and this morning’s unanimous “welcome back”?

According to Nvidia’s official announcement, two things broke the deadlock: a series of sitdowns where the board became “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead,” and — crucially — a green light from Washington.

The board explicitly noted that it “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

Combine that quiet federal clearance with an internal employee revolt, vocal backing from the White House and a brutal month on the stock ticker, and the board’s math became pretty simple.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Jones said in Monday’s statement, thanking Colette Kress for holding the fort as interim CEO before returning to her full-time CFO duties.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Huang, for his part, struck a notably humbler tone than the usual keynote bravado I’ve seen in person a few times.

"I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment... Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can't wait to get back to work." — Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO.

In a recent development, before you get too excited with “WE ARE SO BACK” responses and “stonks” GIFs, read the fine print at the bottom of Nvidia’s press release. Huang may have his title back, but he’s walking back into a very different corporate structure — and the legal storm hasn’t magically evaporated:.

If you were hoping that two weeks of boardroom chaos at Nvidia would pop the AI bubble and magically bring back $90 DDR5 kits (like me), I have some bad news: Jensen Huang’s comeback just put the AI infrastructure train right back at full throttle.

With Wall Street cheering his return and Washington clearing the runway, hyperscalers aren’t tapping the brakes on data center spending anytime soon.

That means Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron have zero reason to pull wafers off high-margin data center memory and send them back to everyday PC builders — especially with Trendforce expecting DRAM prices to climb another 10-15% this quarter and stay tight well into 2027.

Does that mean the dream of RAMageddon dying is gone? Not quite — it just changes your game plan.

According to recent reports, if you see a legitimate Black Friday deal that actually undercuts pre-crisis pricing, treat it like an escape hatch. Waiting for “cheaper RAM next spring” is a gamble that’s looking worse by the hour.

According to recent reports, there is one genuine silver lining. While DRAM stays squeezed, Trendforce’s latest forecast shows NAND flash prices finally turning the corner and starting to dip as early as Q1 2027 — so unless you spot a genuinely fair Black Friday deal, don’t let retailers gouge you on storage right now.

Nvidia’s rebound might keep AI demand humming, but it doesn’t bail the memory giants out of their California antitrust lawsuit or stop the mainstream backlash over inflated PC prices.

Jensen getting his desk back is great news for Nvidia shareholders. For the rest of us just trying to buy a computer without paying an absurd memory tax, the message is simple: grab the real Black Friday bargains while they exist, ignore the fake red discount stickers, and buckle in — RAMageddon isn’t packing its bags just yet.

#97268. AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 26m • 📚 Deep Dive (5192 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.
  • Data centers already use light in networking.
  • The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

Data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

It has been revealed that the reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” states Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

“I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” notes Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in Newly introduced Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon indicates this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.

The startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the firm’s tech to beat GPUs.

Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr states.

It has been revealed that to accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

Industry observers note that the startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” states Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”.

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

According to recent reports, bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”.

According to recent reports, the approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen states, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The tech giant is at the moment choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

In a recent development, both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr claims. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”.

In a recent development, free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another significant advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

Recent findings suggest that “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” indicates Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

Industry observers note that one way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

Recent findings suggest that in Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

It has been revealed that Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the manufacturer declared a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Industry observers note that not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

In a recent development, “A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” claims Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

Industry observers note that even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the manufacturer believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch notes.

The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the manufacturer’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

Recent findings suggest that lightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

Recent findings suggest that lightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

Sources indicate that lightSolver’s team is right now working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the firm’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi notes. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

According to recent reports, yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick Newly introduced, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” Upcoming says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis.

According to recent reports, instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

According to recent reports, some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

Fresh notes that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

In a recent development, how likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he says. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

According to recent reports, however, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Claims Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” states Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

DeepMind’s AI agents found cheaper quantum algorithms, and proved them

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google DeepMind’s illustration for its research on AI-discovered quantum algorithms.
  • Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI used teams of Gemini 4 agents to find more efficient quantum algorithms for fusion, chemistry and drug-design problems.
  • Google DeepMind claims teams of AI agents have found faster quantum algorithms for problems in fusion energy, chemistry and drug design.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google DeepMind’s illustration for its research on AI-discovered quantum algorithms.

Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI used teams of Gemini 4 agents to find more efficient quantum algorithms for fusion, chemistry and drug-design problems. Each result was proved correct in the Lean theorem prover, because the circuits are too large to test on today’s computers.

Google DeepMind claims teams of AI agents have found faster quantum algorithms for problems in fusion energy, chemistry and drug design. The agents, running on Gemini 4, proved each result correct with Lean, a tool that checks mathematical proofs, the lab remarked on Monday.

The proofs matter because the circuits are too big to test. They need thousands of qubits, far beyond what classical computers can simulate or today’s quantum chips can run.

The biggest gain came in a fusion problem. The agents cut the cost of a quantum calculation for laser-driven fusion fuel by 11.8 times, and its memory from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits, DeepMind notes.

Sources indicate that they also made a simulation of a light-sensitive molecule about eight times cheaper. For Cytochrome P450, an enzyme that breaks down most medicines, the cost fell 2.5 times. A widely used maths routine became more than 290 times cheaper.

Sources indicate that separate agent teams worked on each problem and shared verified ideas in a common notebook. Every four hours, they met in a virtual conference to debate and compare approaches. The work, with Google Quantum AI, used Google’s most powerful model, Gemini 4 Carbon.

An outside checker re-ran every proof so agents could not game the tests, according to the paper. That risk is real: in a DeepMind experiment in September, 14% of agents cheated on Lean maths problems.

DeepMind cautions that the simulations would still need far more resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers will offer. It has open-sourced its Lean library and results, building on its 2024 work to trim quantum circuits with AlphaTensor-Quantum. Earlier this month, its agents also proved Signal’s encryption code correct, and Google Quantum AI tested a key quantum effect on up to 105 qubits.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A few years ago, CUB3D demonstrated unsigned code execution on the iPod nano 6G and 7G through ipod_sun, a font-based exploit.
  • I wanted to get Rockbox running on the nano 5G, so I set out to adapt the exploit.
  • In a recent development, existing DFU exploits, including q3kâs wInd3x, provide code execution on the nano 5G, but booting custom code this way requires a computer each time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A few years ago, CUB3D demonstrated unsigned code execution on the iPod nano 6G and 7G through ipod_sun, a font-based exploit. Whether the same approach would work on the 5G was still an open question.

I wanted to get Rockbox running on the nano 5G, so I set out to adapt the exploit. My motivation was simple: an up-to-date music player without an internet connection. I built a fully untethered boot chain that loads Rockbox from the nano 5Gâs NAND, with no computer or button sequence needed after installation. I also found a way to make the existing exploit fully untethered on the nano 7G, and likely the 6G too.

In a recent development, existing DFU exploits, including q3kâs wInd3x, provide code execution on the nano 5G, but booting custom code this way requires a computer each time. I used wInd3x to explore the device and develop a convenient, fully untethered exploit. The firmware details below refer to the latest nano 5G firmware, 1.0.2 (34A20020).

The nano 5Gâs NAND flash appears through a flash translation layer (FTL) as a logical disk with 4 KiB sectors. Its partition table separates a small private area for persistent device state, a firmware partition containing boot programs and resources, and a data volume for user files. The firmware partition has a directory of named images; the fonts live inside rsrc, a resource volume formatted as FAT16.

The original ipod_sun chain combines a resource-validation bypass with a font-parser vulnerability. Appleâs firmware directory identifies the normal operating system as osos, the disk-mode program as disk, and the resource image containing fonts as rsrc. The disk-mode boot path does not request the resource signature check used by normal OS boot.

In a recent development, swapping the disk and osos directory entries exploits that difference: selecting disk mode now releases Appleâs regular OS under the disk-mode policy. The OS still reads its fonts, but the bootloader has not required a valid signature for the modified resource image.

It has been revealed that the font then triggers CVE-2010-1797, the FreeType CFF stack-overflow vulnerability also known through the star exploit. A malformed font program corrupts the parserâs stack and redirects execution. My 5G port adapts that technique to the deviceâs font and execution context.

Recent findings suggest that the swapped images remain on disk, but each restart still requires choosing disk mode with the deviceâs buttons. A normal boot selects the other entry. I wanted a better experience, with the modified font loading through the normal OS path.

Sources indicate that the bootloader is organized into EFI-style modules stored as Portable Executable (PE) images. The module that passes execution to the next boot stage decides whether to validate rsrc. It first asks the PrivateData module for FirmwareStatus, which comes from an authenticated record in the private NAND partition.

It has been revealed that the decisive branch is below. This is reconstructed C from the reverse-engineered routine, with unrelated fuse handling and protocol setup omitted.

Industry observers note that A value of 2 returns success before the resource-validation query. Bit 0 must remain clear: it is checked first, so 3 would reject the boot attempt. Tracing the restore OS shows that it sets the status to 1 during firmware transfer and clears it to 0 at the end. This suggests an enhancement-in-progress guard that prevents booting an incomplete installation.

Sources indicate that appleâs resource-mount path writes status 2 only on the first successful boot, after rsrc has passed signature verification. My hypothesis is that this avoids repeating signature verification to shorten boot time or reduce energy use.

This is the second bypass. Instead of disguising the normal OS as disk mode, I can leave the firmware directory alone and supply a valid private record with bit 1 set. The normal boot path then accepts the modified resource image, and its font delivers code execution automatically.

Sources indicate that the record lives in the private partition, identified by MBR type 0x3e. On the 5G layout I examined, the partition begins at logical block 1, with 4 KiB blocks. The bootloader reads a 512-byte header from its start. The status-bearing format begins with the little-endian magic PRVD and has this layout:.

The integrity tag is device-specific, so creating and saving a valid PRVD record requires code execution on that iPod.

The tag is the first 16 bytes of the SHA-1 digest, encrypted with the deviceâs hardware AES UID key, selected through key slot 2. It authenticates the private header, but as the authentication is constructed on device we can falsify it if we have code execution.

It has been revealed that to inspect and enhancement the private partition, I adapted emCORE, an older framework from freemyipodâs earlier iPod exploitation and boot work. It provided an existing USB-controlled environment to extend for the 5G.

I wrote the nano 5G NAND driver and integrated it into emCORE alongside the flash translation layer (FTL) and hardware AES access. Iâll cover the flash memory sequencer subsystem (FMSS), which enables NAND writes, in a future post. The FTL presents logical sectors over physical flash; it is the layer through which I read and write the private record and install the modified font.

It has been revealed that the private-status tool verifies the existing header and tag, constructs the updated record, and obtains its upcoming tag from the device. It rechecks the partition table and header before writing, then flushes the write and reads it back. The tool writes a complete 4 KiB logical sector even though the bootloader only consumes the smaller header. This works on nano 5G hardware.

Recent findings suggest that once the private record and modified font are installed, they remain in NAND across restarts. emCORE and the host computer are needed for the installation workflow, not for each subsequent boot.

According to recent reports, reaching the font parser automatically solved persistence. The next constraint was fitting something useful inside the font. I wanted it to load Rockbox from storage, so the payload needed a NAND driver, a flash translation layer, a filesystem reader, and enough startup code to hand off reliably.

To fit, I compiled with size and link-time optimizations and had the linker remove unused sections. The Rockbox kernel is stored on the deviceâs FAT32 partition and can be easily updated.

It has been revealed that code execution initially arrives in a damaged FreeType call frame. The stack has been corrupted, and Appleâs OS has left interrupts, DMA controllers, timers, caches, and address translation configured for its own use. Jumping straight into a large C program would carry that state into storage initialization.

I split the bootstrap into two images. The first is the 808-byte assembly stub at 0x22050000. Its job is to leave the parser context: mask IRQs and FIQs, switch to a private stack, stop inherited timer activity, quiesce DMA and clock domains, and clean up caches and the MMU before entering the main payload. It replaces the damaged stack and then jumps to the Rockbox kernel loader.

It has been revealed that the second image is the main loader at 0x22060000. Its entry code disables the watchdog before starting the NAND scan, installs its own stack, and clears the uninitialized-data area before calling C. The watchdog matters because reconstructing the logical flash mapping can take several seconds; a reset in the middle would stop the boot before it ever found Rockbox.

Industry observers note that this separation keeps the most fragile stage small. The assembly stub establishes a controlled execution environment; the main payload can then do the more substantial storage work in freestanding C.

Sources indicate that at the hardware level, the NAND driver uses FMSS, a programmable microcontroller, to communicate with the NAND chips. lemonjesusâs earlier work on the S5L8702 sequencer, published as S5L8702-FMISS-Tools, documents its instruction set and provides tools for inspecting and building bytecode. That research is important prior work for understanding this part of the storage hardware; my work here uses the sequencer to read NAND as part of the nano 5G boot path.

It has been revealed that the loader first checks that the microsecond timer used for driver timeouts is running. It then initializes the read-only NAND and FTL stack, mounts the FAT filesystem, and opens /.rockbox/rockbox.ipod. The core sequence follows the Rockbox bootloaderâs own file-loading path:.

Sources indicate that the file loader checks the Rockbox model identifier and checksum, then leaves the executable image at 0x08000000. The final handoff keeps interrupts masked, cleans and invalidates caches, drains pending writes, and branches to that address. Rockboxâs startup code takes over from there. If storage, mounting, or image loading fails, the payload highlights the failing stage on the LCD and stops.

On my nano 5G, the result is a cold, battery-powered boot straight into Rockbox, with no USB connection and no disk-mode button sequence. The PRVD partition setting skips rsrc validation and, when combined with the star exploit, enables untethered boot straight into Rockbox. The main constraint is that the font payload is limited to 27,874 bytes. Installation and restoration procedures, along with the reverse-engineering notes and build details, are in the nano5g_bootstub and nano5g_emCORE repositories below.

I have confirmed that the private-data partition works the same way on the nano 7G, which suggests the method will likely work on the 6G too. I plan to get the nano 4G and 5G Rockbox ports into good shape before applying this method to the 6G and 7G.

After reviewing close to 100 coffee makers in the last 5 years, we've yet to find a machine that can beat the formidable Technivorm Moccamaster KBGV Select. Durable, consistent and iconic for a reason, it's back at the top of our guide after we re-reviewed it in early 2026.

But while we think the Moccamaster is the best coffee maker for most people, there are so many types and brands of coffee maker to choose from. If you're looking for a great espresso machine, it's the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch we recommend above all others. Its compact design and advanced features combine customisable elements with a user-assisted interface that will make it easy to craft delectable espresso.

I've been reviewing coffee makers for over six years, and I never log on for a day of work without two shots of espresso in my system. An SCA-certified barista, I've tested everything from a $9 French press to a $3,000 espresso machine. I'd happily drink a brew made in any of the seven machines I've featured in my carefully-curated list of the best coffee makers. So if you want an expert-approved brewer, just keep scrolling.

It has been revealed that it's late November, which means Black Friday deals are live. Our on-page tech in this guide will show you when there are discounts on our favorite machines, but if you're looking for more coffee deals over the holiday season, we're continually updating our roundup of the best Black Friday deals, including coffee makers like the Keurig K-Express which is almost half price right now. Or, if you're after inspiration for the enthusiast in your life, these are the best gifts for coffee lovers this holiday season.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Industry observers note that we've reviewed nearly a dozen coffee makers so far this year, and most notably, reviewer Erin re-tested the iconic Moccamaster, which we last put through its paces back in 2021. We wanted to see if it still held its own against the many outstanding releases of the last few years. And the answer is a resounding yes. Now back at the top of our guide, it's certainly the one to beat for the rest of the year's top releases.

Compiling this buying guide has required a lot of evaluation and comparison between completely unrelated methods of brewing, as well as machines that span from $50 to well over $2,000. How, you might wonder, can we rank these machines if they're being tested against completely different criteria?

It's true, I'd never tell you to buy a drip coffee maker if you love espresso, and we'd never tell you to buy the most premium machine if you're on a budget, so before you buy, you need to have a rough idea of what kind of coffee you actually want to make at home.

In this guide, I've included drip coffee makers, as well as a range of single-serve machines and espresso machines. And when ranking these products, I've considered what's right for most people. I know a lot more about coffee than the majority of buyers, so I had to go back to basics when writing this guide to make it accessible to everyone.

Industry observers note that even within the Tom's Guide team, there's a huge range of coffee preferences. There are some people who would turn their nose up at a cup of pod coffee, and would never consider straying from their carefully evaluated coffee setup.

For others, coffee is simply a tool for waking up in the morning, and you just want a reliable and space-efficient gadget to fill your cup with something cheaper and better than the stuff you'd get from a chain coffee shop. That's ok too, because you know your budget, and you know what you're looking for. And no matter what it is that you're seeking, I'm confident that I've included it in this guide.

Each and every machine has been hand-selected and tested by myself or one of Tom's Guide's expert testers, so you can click through to read full, detailed reviews before you make up your mind.

It has been revealed that the Technivorm Moccamaster KBGV Select has been in this buying guide for five years, but a lot has changed since our first review in 2021. So in early 2026, we took it for another spin to see if it can hold its own against the latest and greatest releases.

In a recent development, well, the results are in, and the Moccamaster is still the cream of the crop. Hand-made in the Netherlands, the brand has a well-deserved reputation for quality construction and dependable results. It's not the cheapest option, but if you treat it with care, it will last a lifetime.

Industry observers note that reviewer Erin remarked "the Moccamaster is so famous because nothing really compares. Nothing comes close. The Moccamaster has been topping “best-of” lists before best-of lists were even a thing — it’s reigned supreme since the ‘60s.".

Compared to feature-rich options like the Ratio Four, Breville Luxe Brewer, or OXO Brew 8-Cup, the Moccamaster stands out for its simplicity and efficiency. It forgoes extras like cold brew modes or app controls, but it’s faster than the Ratio Four, easier to use than the Breville Luxe Brewer, and delivers a more consistent cup than the OXO. The machine offers simplicity and ease of use in everyday drip brewing.

To use, simply add your water to the tank and your grounds to the filter, and switch it on. However, it's this simplicity that has earned special recognition from the Specialty Coffee Association. Using a copper heating element and precise brew temperature control, the KBGV Select can hit industry-standard temperatures between 196°F and 205°F in under a minute and, crucially, stay there throughout the entire brewing process. The gentle showerhead-style water dispenser will evenly agitate coffee grounds to create a balanced extraction.

The Breville Bambino Plus has been on the market for seven years, but it's still one of the most popular espresso machines ever released. If you're based in Europe (like me) you'll know this brand as Sage, but the machines are otherwise the same.

With groundbreaking automatic steaming technology, which is still top of the line nearly a decade later, this is the espresso machine for you if you're in the market for an entry-level machine with some serious power.

We made some outstanding shots of espresso with this gadget. I'm talking drool-worthy toffee-colored strands of crema and a vibrant extraction that tasted fantastic. You should note, this machine doesn't have a grinder built in.

You'll want to pair it with one of the best coffee grinders (you can buy a good one for around $100, and our reviews walk you through all the options) for the ideal espresso, but if you use a double-walled portafilter you can still achieve a lively brew when using pre-ground coffee.

As for the automatic milk steaming, this thing can achieve a very fine micro-foam that's totally latte art-worthy, completely hands-free. And it automatically purges after each use, which will keep the steam wand clog-free and running smoothly (so long as you descale regularly).

It has been revealed that if you want a single-serve coffee maker that can truly do it all, you should look no further than the Nespresso Vertuo Lattissima. Featuring a separate milk dispenser that offers milk-only drinks and two lengths of milk add-ins to any coffee size you opt for, the beauty of this machine is in its simplicity.

You can simply store the milk dispenser in the refrigerator when it's not in use, and you'll get the joys of the entirety of Nespresso's six-size Vertuo system if you prefer a long black coffee or an espresso to start the day.

Recent findings suggest that we enjoyed the thoughtful touches such as an adjustable cup holder to work with any beverage size, and the ability to rinse out the milk dispenser after each use. We did wish that there were more than one milk froth level available, because if you prefer a firmer layer to make an espresso or a softer latte-style steamed milk, you won't be able to adjust this using the Nespresso.

In a recent development, because this machine is part of the Vertuo line it will automatically brew the optimum drink length for each drink and you can enjoy an ever-evolving list of capsules to mix up your routine. We even tried a cold-brew capsule, which was impressively realistic.

It has been revealed that sometimes, simple is better. The OXO Brew 8-Cup is one such machine. It's shy on buttons and limited on features, but this machine undeniably makes tasty coffee, and it's SCA-certified to prove it.

In a recent development, you can brew either 2-4 cups or 5-8 cups with the OXO Brew. It simply requires you to fill up the water tank to your desired cup amount, load up a filter and coffee grounds, then hit start.

According to recent reports, there's beauty in the simplicity, though. Its rainshower distribution ensures that grounds are soaked evenly and consistently before extraction, meaning you won't be left with anemic or muddy coffee, and your coffee will never taste burnt from uncontrolled water temperatures.

Another plus is the double-walled carafe. This will keep your brew hot for a couple of hours, making it ideal for busy households. Reviewer Camryn's only complaint was the water tank, which can't be removed. That's annoying, but it's nothing a jug can't fix.

It has been revealed that somehow, the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch manages to be both super-smart and aesthetically pleasing, while also compact enough for small kitchens. It's no mean feat, and one that won the machine the top spot in our best espresso machine buying guide.

The main addition is the responsive 3.5-inch touchscreen, which walks you through everything from dialing in your beans (finding the right grind size for your specific brew) to automatically steaming the milk for the drink of your choosing.

While there are plenty of excellent automatic features here, this machine also lets you take the reins, which will be a welcome feature for those who want to work on their home barista skills. I enjoyed hand-steaming with this machine, and was able to toggle with finer features to really master every espresso.

In a recent development, it's a small feature, but De'Longhi should take a bow for how compact the La Specialista Touch is. It slotted easily onto my countertops, which often look drowned by larger coffee makers. And despite its compact size, it still does literally everything you could want from an espresso machine.

According to recent reports, while it looks like a drip coffee maker, the Ratio Four is actually an automated pour-over coffee maker. So if you love pour-over, but don't love the laborious process of brewing it, the Ratio Four is for you.

With a sleek, minimalist appearance and straightforward operation, the Ratio took just under seven minutes to brew a 20-ounce serving of coffee, and one cup was complete in three and a half minutes.

Reviewer Erin recommends this option for serious coffee lovers. She called it "sophisticated enough to excite even the most fastidious coffee shop hipster," noting that "if you’re familiar with coffee bean varieties and the phrases “pre-infusion” and “optimal flow rate” don’t scare you off, this is the machine for you.".

Sources indicate that the main downside of this brewer is its lack of 'keep warm' setting. Unlike your average drip brewer, it's not designed with bulk brewing in mind. This one's for the true coffee enthusiasts, who would never dream of reheating a precious V60 brew. If you do want a keep-warm option, check out the Moccamaster or Breville Luxe.

In a recent development, the Terra Kaffe Demi is a standout choice for those who want café-quality drinks at home with zero fuss. Its intuitive interface and one-touch operation make espresso simple, so you can enjoy impressive coffee without mastering barista skills or fiddling with settings.

There are downsides to superautomatic espresso machines, which is why few have scored highly in our rigorous Barista-led testing. But where the locked-away grinding, brewing and steaming mechanisms may feel restrictive for coffee enthusiasts, if your key concern is reliability and ease of use, you can't go wrong with the likes of the Terra Kaffe.

In a recent development, machines that require manual tamping or careful monitoring, such as the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch, can't match the Demi's ease of use. Simply press a button, add your beans, and it will craft anything from a piping hot espresso to a long black Americano in minutes. There's one major con: it doesn't have a milk frother, which many superautomatic machines from the likes of Jura and De'Longhi do offer.

According to recent reports, for anyone who wants the easiest possible coffee routine, the Demi’s accessible cleaning features are a relief. After a month of daily use, review Dan found maintenance practically painless. Pop out the brew group for a rinse, and you’re done. If you want hands-off, great-tasting espresso with minimal upkeep, the Demi delivers. But if you're a coffee lover who knows their arabica from their robusta, its lack of customisation may prove frustrating.

Industry observers note that I joined Tom's Guide in 2024 on the product reviews team. While I test everything from keyboards to vacuum cleaners, I'm also a former barista with years and years of experience, which is why I'm Tom's Guide's go-to coffee maker tester.

I've tested a number of leading espresso machines from Smeg and KitchenAid, as well as other brewing methods such as the AeroPress. I've also been down to Smeg and La Pavoni HQ to get hands-on with some high-tech gear.

I’m Tom’s Guide's Reviews Editor and I’ve been an espresso enthusiast for almost a decade now.

Sources indicate that as a former chef, I started using commercial espresso machines to make tiramisu while working in an Italian restaurant, and that’s where my fascination with 9-bar pressure began. And it hasn’t stopped since.

These days, I spend large chunks of my day testing out the latest and greatest coffee gear, from coffee grinders and weighing scales through to pour-over drippers and, of course, coffee machines.

In a recent development, at the end of the day, the most important sign of a good coffee maker comes down to that all-important taste test. So it goes without saying that I taste a lot of coffee when putting together my coffee maker reviews. However, there are endless factors that can determine the flavor of your finished coffee, so there are some metrics I need to consider (and keep consistent) when testing coffee makers and curating buying guides.

Recent findings suggest that the most sustainable choice you can make when buying a fresh coffee maker is opting for a machine that will last for years and years. That stated, it's a good sign when a coffee maker comes in recyclable, sustainable packaging that still keeps it secure during shipping, so I'm always looking out for this when evaluating my first impressions of a product.

Sources indicate that in my experience, a more drawn-out setup process can be worth the extra hassle. Some coffee makers have a water hardness strip included to input the limescale level in your water. This test takes a few extra minutes, but inputting this information will ensure the machine reminds you to descale it as and when needed to prolong its lifespan.

If a coffee maker comes with an app or any bespoke programming such as personalized profiles or pre-set timers, we troubleshoot this in testing to make sure you're getting an easy-to-use machine from the very first use.

Coffee makers don't have to be expensive — especially if you're buying a single-serve or drip coffee maker, but it's often the case that you get what you pay for with coffee makers. When testing I evaluate if this is the case. Does a $1,000+ coffee maker really warrant the price tag, and most importantly, would I recommend it to a friend or family member who was shopping for a newly introduced machine?

Your cup of coffee can only be as good as the grounds you use, so when testing, I try and opt for an accessible consumer blend and stick to this brand across models to ensure that the differences we taste in our coffee come from the quality of the machine, and not the beans.

As a basic rule, I use fresh-roasted arabica beans in every review. This allows the taste and extraction of every coffee to shine through. And while I don't expect that every home tester will be splashing out on artisan beans, at least this way you know you're getting a machine that can create some seriously tasty coffee if you ever decide to level up from those kilo bags of robusta.

According to recent reports, this is particularly crucial for drip coffee makers. I test the temperature of each carafe I make when it's first brewed, and then after one hour, to test the quality of the heating plate on each machine.

In a recent development, if freshly brewed coffee comes out too hot, it's a sign that the machine has scorched the grounds in testing, which will result in a more bitter flavor and is a sign of a poorly-made machine. Likewise, if the coffee is not hot enough, you won't get a fully developed flavor and your coffee will be weak and acidic.

Some coffee makers come with in-built grinders, so I put them through a similar process to our standalone reviews for the best coffee grinders. This involves testing the variety of grind sizes available, and how suitable this is for the type of coffee maker you're using. If your espresso maker's grinder creates great grounds for filter coffee, that's not much help!

I use a coffee sifter called Kruve to see how consistent the coffee grounds are in size and texture, and we also test coffee grinders for static.

Industry observers note that if an espresso machine comes with a hand milk steamer, there is an inevitable margin for user error when testing. Fortunately, I have a team of expert testers on-hand who have steamed more than a few lattes in their time, so if they find fault with a steamer, I can confidently say it's a flaw in design.

When steaming milk, I look for a smooth and fine micro-foam that doesn't burn the milk before we're able to get the consistency we want.

Some machines come with automatic frothers, and while it's hard for these to recreate a hand-steaming effect, I look for how easy they are to use and how close they come to the real thing.

If all of this seems a bit overwhelming, we've tried to simplify the category a bit and help you decide on which type of coffee maker you should buy.

We test a lot of coffee makers. It feels like there's always a new innovation to put through its paces, so our testing team can be found reliably caffeinated on any given day.

We return most of the coffee makers we test due to the high value of these machines, but on the occasion that we're allowed to keep one, we continue to test them from home in order to evaluate the value for money over time, and compare our old faithfuls to recent releases.

Not every coffee maker can make the list though. Here are some of the models we've recently tried.

The xBloom is one of the most interesting drip coffee makers on the market, with legions of fans who love getting involved with every step of the brewing process.

Read the full xBloom Drip Coffee Maker review.

Gevi 10-Cup Drip Coffee Maker (★★☆☆☆).

Let's just say Erin did not enjoy the Gevi. Its in-built grinder is really, really bad, which means it's impossible to get a decent brew out of this machine.

Read the full Gevi 10-Cup Drip Coffee Maker review.

Smeg EMC02 Mini Pro Manual Espresso Machine (★★★★☆).

Sources indicate that smeg teamed up with La Pavoni, makers of the original espresso machine, to create the EMC02. And it lives up to the hype. In testing, Erin found that it's the closest she's got to professional equipment at home.

Read the full Smeg EMC02 Mini Pro Manual Espresso Machine review.

According to recent reports, erin described the De'Longhi Rivelia as a coffee-making robot. This superautomatic does it all, from grinding your beans to order to frothing just the right amount of milk for your desired drink. Its smart interface is what sets it apart, with different user profiles allowing you to interact with the machine depending on everything from your go-to drink to the time of day. We couldn't add it to the guide because, while it's very well-priced in the U.K., the price in America is a bit exorbitant for what you get.

Nespresso Vertuo Pop Plus (★★★★☆).

According to recent reports, there's only so good Nespresso coffee can taste, so you may as well get one of the brand's cheaper machines, especially if you're not concerned with milk-based drinks. The Pop+ is compact and cute to look at, but it drips a lot and won't fit every mug. If you're looking for a neat little machine, it's a savvy option — especially if you find it on sale.

Amazon-favorite brand Casabrews offers suspiciously affordable espresso machines which certainly look the part, but can they deliver? Surprisingly, they kind of can. It has been revealed that you won't find a Keurig in this guide. But some people love Keurig, and we've got a dedicated best Keurig coffee maker guide just for those people. The K-Duo Hot & Iced is the winner in that guide, scoring a 4.5-star review.

Philips Barista Brew Espresso Machine (★★★☆☆).

It has been revealed that ninja's coffee maker wants to be your one-stop shop for all kinds of coffee drinks. But not all its creations are of equal quality, with cold drinks suffering in particular.
