Danger Without SuperintelligenceThe intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.3. A Useful AI FuturePowerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s key to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky swiftly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.” Explore the Superintelligence Debate In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a fresh instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the firm’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

In a recent development, these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

Industry observers note that in the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

Industry observers note that the misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Sources indicate that consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its customers because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted intends for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

In a recent development, even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

In a recent development, this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

Sources indicate that what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The biggest issue with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat.
  • MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.
  • Sources indicate that heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest issue with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Sources indicate that heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker says it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

The result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

According to recent reports, the MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

Sources indicate that the single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

One thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker says that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

Anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

There’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also quickly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

It has been revealed that qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I said in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

Tech Report: If Inflation Stays Hot, These 5 ETFs Could Be Smart Buys

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 10 stocks we like better than Schwab Strategic Trust - Schwab U.s.
  • Sources indicate that if you fill your gas tank or buy groceries, you undoubtedly understand how inflation erodes the purchasing power of cash.
  • According to recent reports, while no exchange-traded fund (ETF) is a guaranteed inflation shield, some do a better job than others at protecting your portfolio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Dana George – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:45PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Schwab Strategic Trust - Schwab U.s. Tips ETF ›.

Sources indicate that if you fill your gas tank or buy groceries, you undoubtedly understand how inflation erodes the purchasing power of cash. And if you invest, you may be on the lookout for assets that can help cushion your portfolio.

According to recent reports, while no exchange-traded fund (ETF) is a guaranteed inflation shield, some do a better job than others at protecting your portfolio. Here are five of them.

SCHP invests in Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS). The principal adjusts with inflation, helping preserve purchasing power, and pays interest on that adjusted principal.

Recent findings suggest that TIPS can help preserve purchasing power over time. However, a TIPS value may fluctuate if market prices fall.

According to recent reports, VTIP is a shorter-duration alternative. During inflationary times, VTIP may be less sensitive to interest rate changes than funds holding longer-term bonds because it focuses on shorter-maturity TIPS.

If you seek inflation-linked bonds with less duration risk, VTIP is worth considering. Keep in mind, though, the fund still carries risk, and returns depend on both inflation adjustments and changes in bond prices.

Switching to yet another kind of exposure, PDBC invests in commodity futures across markets, such as agriculture, metals, and energy. Commodities are closely tied to costs that often drive inflation, so they may perform well when raw material prices rise.

However, commodity prices can swing sharply, and futures-based funds naturally face complexities that you may not be accustomed to.

Industry observers note that gold is viewed as a way to preserve wealth over time. Unlike cash, it can't be created at will, and gold may rise in value as cash loses purchasing power. Gold can also help balance a portfolio loaded with stocks and bonds.

On the downside, gold is not directly tied to the CPI and can fall even while inflation remains elevated. In addition, its performance may lag when interest-bearing assets become more attractive.

Still, investing in GLDM is one way to diversify risk.

XLE holds energy sector companies, so if oil and gas prices rise, the fund's value may rise, making it a hedge against inflation.Yet energy stocks are still stocks, and regulation, manufacturer costs, demand, and even market sentiment can outweigh the effect of higher fuel prices.

Industry observers note that while each of these funds can be a great addition to your portfolio as inflation heats up, they're not interchangeable. SCHP and VTIP focus on inflation-linked government bonds, while PDBC tracks a collection of commodity futures. GLDM provides gold exposure, while XLE invests in energy companies.

Each ETF responds to inflation through a different mechanism, and while each can help, they can all disappoint if the market moves the other way.

The takeaway is to treat inflation-focused ETFs as possible portfolio pieces rather than all-in solutions. Before investing, consider fees, diversification, tax treatment, and how much volatility you can tolerate.

Industry observers note that the holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up….

The Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a significant upgrade last year, adding a variety of fresh higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

Industry observers note that the Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

It has been revealed that even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people newly introduced to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

Recent findings suggest that the Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a big revision over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-new Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the organization conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”.

With the upcoming system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

As I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The new sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

In a recent development, the Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

The Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

Sources indicate that anthropic is launching a newly introduced tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”.

According to recent reports, claude Ship is a new product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

According to recent reports, “That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic says. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic states.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring upcoming challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also highlights how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple TV (now $6.99/month for limited time) has just announced that Ted Lasso will return for season 5.
  • This summer Apple TV aired the highly anticipated return of Ted Lasso.
  • Season 4 debuted three full years after the last season ended, and brought a fresh start to one of the streamer’s all-time most beloved series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple TV (now $6.99/month for limited time) has just announced that Ted Lasso will return for season 5. Here are the details.

This summer Apple TV aired the highly anticipated return of Ted Lasso.

Season 4 debuted three full years after the last season ended, and brought a fresh start to one of the streamer’s all-time most beloved series.

But after the season 4 finale aired, Apple provided no indication whether the show would continue or not.

Now, uncertainty around the show’s fate is over.

Apple has revealed that Ted Lasso season 5 is officially coming.

Following its hit fourth season, Apple’s global phenomenon “Ted Lasso” is officially returning back to the pitch for season five. Starring and executive produced by Emmy Award winner Jason Sudeikis, the fourth season of “Ted Lasso” introduced the Lady Greyhounds, with critics hailing it as “a perfect setup for a fresh return” and “one of the most beloved comedy demonstrates of the decade.”.

The announcement is light on further details. However, there should be a much shorter wait for season 5 than there was for season 4.

In a recent development, before Ted Lasso returned this year, Jason Sudeikis shared that he had a new three-season arc in mind. Apple’s Eddy Cue also suggested the company would be happy to continue making more seasons for years to come.

But until today’s announcement, the lack of official news still put Lasso fans’ hopes on pause.

Whether it returns in 2027 or, perhaps more likely 2028, Ted Lasso isn’t going away again anytime soon.

Are you excited for Ted Lasso’s season 5 renewal? Let us know in the comments.

Apple TV is available for just $6.99/ month (over 50% off) for a limited time, with the offer ending Monday, November 30.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • September ended on a mixed note, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 0.5% and 4.3%, respectively, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.9%.
  • In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects.
  • Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

September ended on a mixed note, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 0.5% and 4.3%, respectively, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.9%. Markets remained on edge with higher oil prices and Treasury yields weighing on investor sentiment and triggering fears of additional interest rate hikes.

In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Neocloud company CoreWeave (CRWV) is benefiting from robust AI-driven demand for cloud computing.

Industry observers note that recently, JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee upgraded CoreWeave to buy from hold, raising his price target to $125 from $120. The analyst cited favorable pricing, driven by solid demand, for the upgrade.

Chatterjee noted CoreWeave is now more willing to sign premium priced, shorter-term contracts, which lift his revenue and margin estimates. CRWV stock performance has been underwhelming as investors worry about high capital spending, the analyst noted. That said, he believes that higher prices and increased margins will more than offset the rise in debt to fund capital spending, improving the stock's valuation.

Chatterjee noted the 25% price hike in July across CoreWeave's product offerings and frequent price increases by rivals like Nebius (NBIS), adding that some peers are charging nearly three times more for short-term compute contracts than what CoreWeave charges on longer-term deals.

"CoreWeave's leverage of the opportunity [is] evident in its recent press release highlighting contracts signed in F3Q at ~$40M/MW," remarked Chatterjee. JPMorgan said higher pricing is already contributing 5-10 percentage points to contract margins versus earlier deals.

Chatterjee ranks No. 4 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 55.3%. See CoreWeave Statistics on TipRanks.

It has been revealed that palo Alto Networks (PANW) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404.

Recent findings suggest that after a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%.

Over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and latest markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security tech giant, Powell stated. The 5-star analyst estimates that hardware firewalls and attached subscriptions now account for less than 50% of revenue.

In a recent development, meanwhile, high-growth solutions, including Prisma SASE, software firewalls, Cortex XSIAM, Chronosphere and Idira now represent more than 35% of PANW's revenue. "Investors may not fully realize the growth potential within PANW's platform story," Powell said.

BTIG is optimistic about the prospects of Chronosphere in observability, CyberArk in identity and software firewalls and Prisma AIRS in the network and AI security business.

Powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks.

Recent findings suggest that in a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon (AMZN), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he remarked.

Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

Additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack.

Overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. Fewer clicks would not hurt the manufacturer if the value of each remaining click and overall volumes keep rising, he said. The argument is that even if Amazon loses some sponsored ad revenue over the next few years, it would likely be only a small part of the company's total business and could be offset by growth in other areas.

In a recent development, "Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," said Devitt. His bullish view is supported, Devitt said, by expectations that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will exit the year at a more than 45% growth rate with continued margin improvement.

Devitt ranks No. 765 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 49% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Amazon Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:45PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Align Technology ›.

It has been revealed that on its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 28, 2026, Align (ALGN +4.63%) reported revenue of $1.015 billion, up 1.9% year over year. Clear aligner volume grew as dental practices adopted lower-upfront-cost options to help budget-conscious patients start treatment.

Management shares three key insights on how the manufacturer plans to navigate this environment.

Sources indicate that systems and Services revenue dropped 7.6% year over year as practices shifted toward leasing, rentals, and lower-priced hardware options. Management expects these flexible arrangements to lower adoption hurdles, expand the installed base, and drive recurring software revenue over time.

According to recent reports, the company is applying its direct fabrication technology from orthodontic appliances like palatal expanders into new product lines, starting with custom sports mouthguards. Management aims to leverage this direct fabrication platform to increase brand awareness among younger patients and raise doctor utilization rates.

According to recent reports, manufacturing automation, higher factory productivity, and lower treatment refinement rates lifted non-GAAP operating margin, an adjusted measure that excludes one-time charges, to 24.4%. Financial planning for 2027 relies on internal expense discipline rather than assuming a recovery in discretionary consumer spending.

Soft consumer demand continues to pressure discretionary healthcare spending, but operational execution creates clear pathways to growth across global markets. Expanding digital workflows, deeper relationships with dental service organizations, and proprietary direct fabrication offer structural advantages as hardware pricing stabilizes. Management monitors doctor utilization rates, patient financing adoption, and operating discipline to protect profitability.

According to recent reports, automation efforts and strategic cost reviews support ongoing operational expansion. Management targets steady efficiency gains while funding core digital platforms and returning capital through share repurchases.

#97225. The search for a top dark matter candidate

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2598 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag ↗ Open Full Page

The search for a top dark matter candidate

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Italy’s Gran Sasso National Laboratory is not a bad place to fret over the state of your career.
  • Industry observers note that the lab also descends into the Gran Sasso mountain, forming one of the world’s largest underground research centers.
  • For the past few decades, scientists have been hunting for dark matter, the invisible substance that makes up 85 percent of the matter in our universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Italy’s Gran Sasso National Laboratory is not a bad place to fret over the state of your career. The lab’s panoramic views of white-capped mountains and endless greenery are nearly inescapable. Physicists fuel their work with sharp espressos, rather than the watery coffee many Americans accept.

Industry observers note that the lab also descends into the Gran Sasso mountain, forming one of the world’s largest underground research centers. Nestled beneath 4,600 feet of rock is an array of particle detectors. Thanks to the mountain’s thick skin, these instruments are shielded from cosmic rays, the high-energy particles produced by black holes, exploding stars and even our own sun. In the quiet depths of this laboratory, physicists hope to pick up on much more elusive particles—including dark matter.

For the past few decades, scientists have been hunting for dark matter, the invisible substance that makes up 85 percent of the matter in our universe. One primary target has been weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs—a hypothesized candidate for dark matter that passes through normal matter with barely a trace. Massive underground detectors like those at Gran Sasso are leading the search.

In a recent development, but no one has definitively found a WIMP, so no one is sure that they exist—and challenges to spotting them are building. As detectors get more sensitive, newly introduced background signals are beginning to cloud them, reducing the odds of catching WIMPs. Funding is growing more precarious, leaving many wondering how many years this endeavor has left.

When I visited the lab in May, the mood among some of these physicists was muted. “Of course, we were a bit more depressed,” reflects physicist Paolo Salomone, laughing. Despite his clear enthusiasm for the dark matter hunt, Salomone, a strikingly blue-eyed University of Chicago postdoctoral scholar, knew he was entering a field some might diagnose as terminal.

Then, in September, a pinprick of hope emerged. An American lab also searching for WIMPs released a preprint paper detailing a single—but intriguing—data point, rising above the expected background signals. Maybe, just maybe, it was dark matter.

According to recent reports, salomone was on vacation in Corsica when his phone started blowing up. Text notifications from physicist friends streamed in, asking him if he’d seen the news. “I was there on the beach trying to look at my phone, trying to zoom in on the plot,” he says. Watching the faraway excitement, he says, “I felt like I was missing out a lot.”.

In a recent development, the finding was not a definite dark matter detection—one data point isn’t nearly enough to count as a discovery. Still, the result spawned headlines across the globe, a torrent of preprint papers and newfound hope for many physicists in search of WIMPs.

The question, now, is what’s next. Will this life raft be enough to overcome the field’s growing challenges? And will the few other detectors with similar sensitivity—most notably, one at Gran Sasso—be able to replicate the signal?

Recent findings suggest that nearly a century ago, Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky noticed a group of galaxies with some moving so quickly that they should have escaped the cluster’s gravity and flown apart. He theorized that some invisible material was gluing them together. Since then, scientists have accrued more evidence for this dark matter: stars speeding precipitously fast around a galaxy’s rim; unexpectedly strong gravitational lensing, in which distant light is bent by extreme gravity.

To explain it all, astrophysicists dreamed up WIMPs in the 1980s. As far as subatomic particles go, these would be relatively massive. In theory, they glide through space, on occasion lightly interacting with matter. Physicists have a pretty good sense of the density of dark matter scattered throughout our universe, but not much more about it. “It opens the possibility of having a lot of light particles or very few heavy particles,” states Salomone.

It has been revealed that directly detecting WIMPs, then, could clue us into the mass of individual dark matter particles and the number of them floating around, as well as how strongly these particles interact with normal matter. But finding them has been a challenge. Not only are physicists searching through a vast plain of possibilities, but they’re also looking for incredibly rare interactions that require extreme care in detection.

According to recent reports, the smallest impurities can anger a detector. To illustrate the point, Marcello Messina, the technical coordinator for Gran Sasso’s XENONnT experiment, brought up the humble banana. While we don’t tend to think of a banana as radioactive, the fruits are rich in potassium, leading to a tiny shower of particle decays. “A banana can completely destroy our data table,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that messina was my guide for the day at Gran Sasso, driving me six miles through one of Italy’s longest tunnels and into the mossy interior of the mountain. He led me through the lab’s sterile halls, ending up at his even more sterile detector.

Sources indicate that messina’s XENONnT experiment is a hulking cylinder that holds a chamber of nearly 9.5 tons of xenon—mostly liquid—inside. The hope is that when a WIMP flies into the detector, it jostles one of the large and stable xenon atoms, which would in turn shoot out electrons and a light ray, alerting sensors to the strange particle’s presence.

XENONnT, which has been collecting data for around six years, is the strapping great-grandchild of the team’s original 2006 prototype. “XENON, for almost all its life, provided the most sensitive results,” Messina told me. “It was definitely leading the field.” Today, a few more rivals—like the American detector—have emerged.

According to recent reports, we walked past another device that looked like a gigantic red Lego: a new detector Salomone is helping to build, DarkSide-20k, which will use a chamber of around 55 tons of argon instead of xenon. This enormous detector will reach a similar sensitivity to XENONnT and is set to begin collecting data in 2028.

Recent findings suggest that despite their materials’ purity, physicists expect some level of background fuzz—mainly radioactive decay products—and predict what that will look like. Sometimes, though, this “background” can behave in unexpected ways, so physicists must have a high bar for what anomalies in their data to take seriously.

Messina showed me a kind of memento mori for physicists: the latest generation of the DAMA experiment, which made a claim of dark matter detection that has been dismissed by most of the community.

In 1997, DAMA, which is made up of sodium iodide crystals, detected a signal that varied yearly, swooping in every summer—just as dark matter was expected to do. But while the team has continued to stand by their results, other experiments later ruled this out.

After DAMA’s false alarm, “I think people are just very cautious now,” claims Ina Sarcevic, a physicist at the University of Arizona.

Despite the fear of more detector-cried-wolf scenarios, many physicists swiftly pulled together theories to explain September’s announcement of a possible detection, Sarcevic states. The signal came out of South Dakota’s LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, which is at the moment the world’s largest WIMP detector.

Physicist Richard Gaitskell, LZ’s spokesperson, has been searching for dark matter for nearly 40 years, starting with a detector “barely bigger than the top of my thumb,” he indicates. LZ, on the other hand, is a nine-foot-tall cylinder containing around 11 tons of xenon, packed within a 20-foot-tall outer structure.

To take advantage of LZ’s whopping size and sensitivity, Gaitskell indicates, the team “decided to really aggressively push” beyond the usual search parameters.

The longstanding assumption in these experiments has been that WIMPs swoop in at relatively low energies and bounce off the xenon like billiard balls. In this case, when a WIMP collides with a xenon nucleus, it scatters the atom’s protons and neutrons in what’s called a “coherent” manner, where their resulting energies add up, amplifying the signal. But if WIMPs were to barrel in at higher energies, the particles would scatter in a trickier way to track.

It was the switch to searching for these higher-energy collisions that led to LZ’s unusual detection. The signal also hinted that particles of dark matter would be quite heavy and collide with matter in a different way than many expected. Rather than rebounding like billiard balls, the WIMP may lose some energy (and mass) in the crash, exiting as a different, slimmer form of dark matter.

It has been revealed that notably, this detection couldn’t be explained by known forms of background events, like stray neutrons. The signal, then, could be dark matter, but it may also be a previously unknown type of background.

In announcing this event, Gaitskell claims, the team was looking for input from the wider community, as they continue to pore through their own data. And input he did receive.

In a recent development, amid the excitement and wave of preprint papers, though, many have retained a sense of caution. Messina states he was initially skeptical of the single data point. “The immediate reaction was, ‘Come on, one event?’” he says. But he recognized XENONnT’s potentially crucial role in the next step toward discovery.

Given their detector’s comparable sensitivity, the team is now rushing to replicate the finding, looking through the past two years of their own data for signals that chime with the American detection. Or they could find nothing.

Industry observers note that either way, Messina would like to let the team’s data analysis do the talking, rather than get too excited now. They hope to release a paper in the next few months. “Data matters,” Messina says. “All the rest is fake.”.

According to recent reports, when Messina led me around in the spring, he wasn’t optimistic about the future of his field. He was continuing to support the search for dark matter with XENONnT, but he had also been devoting time to detecting neutrinos, another kind of subatomic particle generated by stars, radioactive decay and the Big Bang. “Many people like me are thinking, ‘You know what, I want to investigate different fields,’” he said.

Some WIMP proponents point out that even though the detectors haven’t found one of these fabled particles, they have made a less obvious kind of progress over the decades. In their searches, scientists have ruled out many potential WIMP masses and densities, ticking away at the options and possibly making it easier to zero in on their true properties in the future.

But to many onlookers—including the funding bodies that control cash flow—the lack of clear progress in particle physics has been disappointing. “It’s quite hard to convince politicians to support you if you have a significant discovery each 30 years,” Messina remarked.

In a recent development, on top of the current fragile science funding ecosystem in the United States, he wasn’t sure how much more time WIMP detection had. He doubted the proposed next-generation detector, XLZD—which would dwarf LZ and XENON and merge the collaborations—would move forward.

After LZ’s finding, though, Messina’s tune has changed. While he still stresses the uncertainty that this signal will lead to a discovery, he believes it has imparted “some momentum” back into WIMPs.

Many physicists still see more promise in other dark matter models—the hypothetical WIMPs might not be the best (or only) explanation.

Ben Safdi, a theoretical physicist at the University of California, Berkeley, indicates that LZ’s detection may well be dark matter, but his initial excitement has waned. At first, the signal seemed to match an existing theory for WIMP behavior, but several preprint papers—including one of his—challenged this idea. “My personal belief that it is dark matter has gone down,” he says.

According to recent reports, safdi divides his research between WIMPs and a different dark matter candidate called axions. These theorized particles would move in a “continuous, almost fluid” wave through the universe, he notes. Individually, axions would be super light—much less massive than WIMPs—but together, they could account for the missing mass of dark matter.

It has been revealed that attention to axions has surged as people have grown tired of WIMPs. While Safdi still thinks the WIMP hunt is worth continuing, “my heart is in axions,” he claims.

Did you know? Other strategies to find WIMPs.

According to recent reports, even if interest in WIMP detection is revitalized, technological challenges remain. One specter still haunting the field is a fog of neutrinos that’s threatening to descend on the instruments.

With increased sensitivity, the detectors are starting to pick up the constant swarm of neutrinos. These tiny particles don’t interact much with matter—trillions move through your body every second—but they can clutter data taken by detectors that are precise enough to notice them. As this neutrino fog wafts in, potential WIMP signals could get lost in the haze. XENONnT reported its first glimpses of the fog in 2024.

Industry observers note that this isn’t a huge problem for the detectors yet, and not everyone agrees it will be soon. But once neutrinos start meaningfully gumming up the signal, scientists don’t know what they’ll do.

In a recent development, ronald Walsworth’s group is experimenting with a workaround: tracing the direction of incoming particles. WIMPs are expected to flood in like a “headwind” against the solar system’s path through the galaxy, he states. On the other hand, a lot of neutrinos emanate from the direction of the sun, produced by the churn of fusion.

A sea of liquid xenon functions “like an antenna,” says Daniel Ang, a quantum scientist in Walsworth’s group. The flash of light only clues scientists into a particle’s collision—not the direction it rode in. So to trace a signal’s source, physicists might have to take a whole newly introduced approach.

Walsworth decided to try this by using a more glamorous substance: diamonds. From his previous work, he knew that when particles cut through diamond crystals, they leave behind a finely detailed track—so their incoming direction is clear. “That’s the grandiose idea we had,” indicates Walsworth, a quantum physicist at the University of Maryland.

But the team has only tested their blinged-out detector on a small scale, and getting the funds to go bigger will be a challenge—especially given the “sagging of enthusiasm” for WIMPs, Walsworth states.

Industry observers note that once Salomone, the postdoc, got back from vacation, his excitement about LZ’s signal was slightly tempered by his boss, he claims. “He was, of course, more skeptical and less enthusiastic than me.”.

But even among Salomone’s liquid argon detector community, scientists are paying serious attention to the result. His collaboration has a regular meeting, which only one or two dozen people usually show up to. But at a recent one, some 100 people attended. Even people who never participated were interjecting with ideas, he says.

Salomone’s workdays are much like before, continuing to help build the DarkSide-20k detector, placing orders for special screws and popping over to the café for an espresso. But he feels a renewed excitement about the theory behind his daily tasks.

“You’re still doing what you were doing before but with a different mind-set,” he says. “Spending more time trying to read papers, spending more time trying to be even a better physicist, so that’s what I’m really happy about.”.

  • Sources indicate that virginia and Oregon filed separate lawsuits on Monday against SpaceX, the parent manufacturer of Grok developer xAI and social media platform X.
  • According to Reuters, these are the first lawsuits brought by U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk's tech giant is facing two new lawsuits over its image-generation capabilities, raising serious questions about what happens when powerful AI tools can manipulate photographs of real people without their permission.

Sources indicate that virginia and Oregon filed separate lawsuits on Monday against SpaceX, the parent manufacturer of Grok developer xAI and social media platform X. Both states allege that the company failed to implement adequate safeguards against the creation of nonconsensual sexual images, including child sexual abuse material.

According to Reuters, these are the first lawsuits brought by U.S. states over the controversy, although several attorneys general have already investigated Grok's image-generation features.

The lawsuits also raise a broader concern for anyone who shares photos online. As AI image generators become more realistic and accessible, how much control do people actually have over what others can create using their pictures?

Here's what happened, what the lawsuits allege and what it could mean for Grok users.

The lawsuits focus on Grok's ability to generate sexualized images and videos from existing photographs.

Industry observers note that grok includes image-generation and editing features that can transform an uploaded photo using text instructions. According to the states, users exploited these capabilities to create explicit or partially nude images of real people without their knowledge or consent.

The complaints specifically point to Grok's controversial "spicy mode," which the states say enabled the generation of sexual content without sufficient protections.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield argue that the manufacturer promoted the safety of its tools while failing to prevent the creation and distribution of harmful images.

The states accuse SpaceX of violating consumer protection laws and are seeking financial penalties, damages and court orders requiring the tech giant to stop the alleged violations.

These are allegations in civil lawsuits, not findings of wrongdoing by a court.

One of the most alarming figures cited in the lawsuits comes from a study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH).

The organization estimated that between December 29, 2025, and January 8, 2026, Grok generated and posted approximately 3 million sexualized images on X, including around 23,000 images that appeared to depict children.

That works out to roughly 190 sexualized images every minute over the study period.

According to recent reports, the figures are estimates from the organization's research rather than a confirmed count of illegal images. Nevertheless, the scale described in the study has become a central part of the states' allegations.

The Virginia Attorney General's Office also alleges that nearly 30% of the sexualized images of children identified in the study remained publicly accessible on X at least a week after they were identified.

Yes. In January 2026, xAI revealed restrictions on Grok's image-editing capabilities, including measures intended to prevent people from generating images of real people in revealing clothing where doing so would be illegal.

However, subsequent reporting raised questions about whether the changes were effective.

In February, Reuters found that Grok could still generate sexualized images of people even when prompts explicitly stated that the subjects had not consented.

The upcoming lawsuits argue that the company's safeguards were inadequate and that its public assurances about user safety were misleading. The company has separately taken legal action against individuals it alleges misused Grok to create child sexual abuse material.

For most customers, the concern goes beyond generating inappropriate AI images.

The lawsuits highlight a growing problem with generative AI: someone may be able to use a photograph of another person to produce realistic fabricated content without that person's permission.

An AI-generated image does not have to depict something that actually happened to cause harm. A convincing fake can be copied, shared or used to harass someone, especially when it circulates on a major social media platform.

The risk is particularly concerning for parents whose children's photos may be publicly accessible online. These lawsuits do not mean that every Grok user has had their photos manipulated, nor do they establish that simply uploading a photo to X causes Grok to generate an explicit image.

Still, they are a reminder that publicly available images can be vulnerable to misuse by people with access to powerful AI editing tools.

Sources indicate that users concerned about this risk can review the visibility of their social media accounts, limit public sharing of sensitive images and report manipulated content when they encounter it. Such precautions cannot eliminate the possibility of misuse, especially when a photograph has already been copied or circulated elsewhere.

Both states are seeking penalties and court orders aimed at stopping the alleged unlawful conduct. The courts have not yet determined whether SpaceX violated either state's consumer protection laws.

The manufacturer also faces more than a dozen lawsuits from individuals who allege that Grok was used to create nonconsensual sexual images of them.

The outcome of the lawsuit could help determine how much responsibility AI companies bear when their tools are used to create harmful images of real people.

But for now, the Grok lawsuits underscore a concern that extends to AI image generation as it has become remarkably powerful, but protecting the people whose likenesses appear in those images remains an unresolved challenge.

iOS 27 brought a variety of major improvements to Shared Albums. And in iOS 27.2, Apple introduced four more.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the problem with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground.

Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.

It has been revealed that I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^).

Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.

We want security nerds to hack it! A upcoming browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves rapidly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.

In a recent development, if you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol.

Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

#97216. Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1824 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Stalw ↗ Open Full Page

Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Stalw

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for more than twenty years, “the mail server” in most companies meant Microsoft Exchange, and “the mail client” meant Outlook.
  • Stalwart now implements the protocols that Exchange clients speak: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover.
  • Exchange support is part of the open source Community edition, under the AGPL.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for more than twenty years, “the mail server” in most companies meant Microsoft Exchange, and “the mail client” meant Outlook. Today we are releasing Stalwart 1.2.0, and with it Stalwart becomes a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange.

Stalwart now implements the protocols that Exchange clients speak: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover. Outlook, Apple Mail and the mail apps on phones and tablets connect to Stalwart as they would to an Exchange server, with mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes in one account. Owners type their email address and password, Autodiscover does the rest, and they keep working in the client they already know.

Exchange support is part of the open source Community edition, under the AGPL.

Before going into what Stalwart now does, it is worth looking at where self-hosted Exchange stands today, because it explains why so many organisations are looking for a way out.

Sources indicate that microsoft has not confirmed the end of Exchange Server. On paper, on-premises Exchange still exists. In practice, every road Microsoft is building leads to Exchange Online:.

None of these steps forces anyone to move on its own. Together, they leave an Exchange administrator with a shrinking set of choices: keep running a server that will not grow, or move the organisation’s mail into Microsoft’s cloud.

It has been revealed that for many organisations the second option is not acceptable. Email is the record of a firm’s contracts, negotiations, legal advice, HR matters and customer data. Placing it with a US provider means placing it within reach of US law, including the CLOUD Act, which allows US authorities to compel American providers to hand over data they control wherever it is stored. Public administrations, healthcare providers, law firms, defence contractors and many European companies cannot accept that, or no longer want to. Data sovereignty means that you decide where your data lives, under which jurisdiction, and who can read it. A mail service in someone else’s cloud cannot offer that, and an on-premises server whose vendor is steering its customers toward that cloud offers less of it every year.

The obstacle to leaving Exchange has rarely been the server. It has been the client.

Many people have spent their whole working life in Outlook. They have years of muscle memory in it: their folder layout, their rules, their calendar views, their shared mailboxes, the way they book meeting rooms. Many organisations also have workflows built around it, such as delegated calendars managed by an assistant. Replacing Exchange with a standard IMAP and CalDAV server has always meant telling every one of those users to switch to a different mail client, or to reconfigure Outlook into a reduced IMAP mode where calendars and contacts no longer sync. For a migration project, that is often where the plan dies.

With Stalwart 1.2.0 the users do not need to change anything. The administrator moves the mailboxes and points the DNS records at Stalwart, and users connect with the same Outlook they used before.

Stalwart implements the following Microsoft protocols, all served on the same HTTPS port as JMAP and the WebUI:.

That set of protocols is what the following clients use to talk to an Exchange server, and they can connect to Stalwart the same way:.

The Exchange protocols are not a separate silo inside Stalwart. They are another door into the same accounts. A message filed in Outlook is in the same mailbox an IMAP or JMAP client sees, a meeting accepted on a phone appears in the calendar that CalDAV clients read, and a contact added in Apple Contacts shows up in the CardDAV address book. A user can keep Outlook on the office desktop, the native mail app on a phone and a JMAP webmail in the browser, all on one account.

Rules created in Outlook’s Rules and Alerts are stored on the server as mail rules, which run as Sieve when the message is delivered. They apply when Outlook is closed and whatever client the user opens next. Delegates and folder permissions set in Outlook become regular Stalwart shares, so they apply to every protocol. Shared mailboxes open automatically in Outlook from group membership, as they do with Exchange.

Not every part of an Exchange deployment has a counterpart. Stalwart does not offer public folders, archive mailboxes, mobile device management, RPC over HTTP (Outlook 2010 and earlier) or NTLM and Kerberos sign-in: clients authenticate with a password, an app password or OAuth. The Exchange documentation covers configuration, DNS and Autodiscover, each family of clients, and the differences from Exchange that administrators should know about before a migration.

One Outlook is missing from the list above: the new Outlook for Windows, the one that Windows now installs by default and that classic Outlook keeps offering through a toggle in its title bar.

The newly introduced Outlook does not work with Stalwart, and it does not work with any self-hosted server, Exchange included. It is built to work through Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft does not support on-premises Exchange accounts in it at all.

The new Outlook does accept IMAP accounts, and that might look like a way around the problem. It is not. When an IMAP account is added to the new Outlook, the connection to the mail server is not made from the user’s computer. As heise and c’t reported in November 2023, the new Outlook sends the IMAP server name, the user name and the password to Microsoft, and Microsoft’s cloud connects to the mail server on the user’s behalf. Every message then passes through Microsoft’s infrastructure on its way to the screen. Microsoft does not only see the mail; it holds the password to the mailbox.

In a recent development, for an organisation that runs its own mail server to keep its data under its own control, this defeats the purpose of the whole exercise. We advise against using the new Outlook with any self-hosted email deployment, whether it runs Stalwart or anything else. Owners who see the “Try the new Outlook” toggle in classic Outlook should leave it off.

Sources indicate that the same applies on phones. Outlook for iOS and Android reach on-premises mailboxes through a Microsoft cloud service as well, which requires a hybrid Exchange Online setup. On mobile devices, the native mail, calendar and contacts apps, which connect directly over ActiveSync, are the better choice.

The obvious question is why Stalwart is adding Exchange protocols now. EWS is being removed from Exchange Online, Microsoft’s own future for Outlook is a cloud client, and classic Outlook is reportedly supported until 2029. Why build support for protocols that will be obsolete in a few years?

Because the companies that run Exchange today cannot wait a few years, and because those protocols are the bridge they need to cross.

An organisation with a few hundred Outlook users cannot replace its mail server and its mail client in the same weekend. It can replace the server, though, if nobody notices. With Stalwart speaking the Exchange protocols, the server moves first: mailboxes are migrated, DNS records change, and on Monday every user opens the same Outlook and the same phone apps they used on Friday. The organisation’s mail is back under its own control from day one, and no one’s work is interrupted to get there.

The client can then change at the pace that suits the users. Over time, as classic Outlook reaches the end of its life and the new Outlook remains tied to Microsoft’s cloud, we expect users to move gradually to third-party email clients built on open standards, and in particular on JMAP. Outlook will stop being an option for anyone who cares about where their email lives, and by then the people who used it will have had the time to choose something else without a deadline over their heads.

According to recent reports, exchange support is not where Stalwart is going. It is how organisations get from where they are to where Stalwart is.

Exchange compatibility is not a small piece of work. It adds about 200,000 lines of code to Stalwart, and we know that some of you would rather not carry that weight if you never proposal to see an Outlook client. We built it with that in mind, so that it costs as little as possible for those who do not use it, and so that it can be removed cleanly once the Exchange protocols are obsolete:.

Recent findings suggest that A drop-in replacement is only useful if the data can follow. Vandelay, our account import and export tool, migrates mailboxes from both sides of Microsoft’s offering:.

Vandelay copies each account into Stalwart over JMAP, and the domain moves to Stalwart when its MX records and client settings change. The migration guide for hosted services walks through the whole process, from the first test account to the cutover. With the Exchange protocols enabled on Stalwart, Outlook and the other Exchange clients then connect through Autodiscover and find the migrated mail, calendars and contacts.

Exchange support is the headline, but 1.2.0 brings several other features, most of them developed alongside it because an Exchange replacement needs them:.

The changelog lists every change and fix, along with the upgrade steps: existing servers need to add the new permissions to their default roles.

Last week we also released version 2.0.0 of stalwart-cli, and its biggest addition is an interactive console. Run stalwart-cli with no arguments in a terminal and it opens a full-screen interface that covers the same ground as the WebUI: browsing and editing accounts, domains and every other configuration object, watching the dashboard, following live traces and running actions. It is aimed at administrators who live in SSH sessions, or who work on hosts where opening a browser is impractical.

The console is built with Ratatui, the excellent Rust library for terminal user interfaces, and it is schema-driven like the rest of the CLI: its screens, forms and field help come from the schema that the server publishes, so it picks up latest objects without being updated. The CLI also learned to sign in with the OAuth device flow and to remember the session, so a single approval in the browser is enough for both the console and every subsequent command.

It has been revealed that stalwart will be at FOSDEM 2027 in Brussels. We will have a Stalwart stand, and on Saturday, 30 January 2027, we will give a talk about moving from Microsoft Exchange to Stalwart in the Modern Email devroom. If you are planning a migration away from Exchange, or are curious about what it takes, come and talk to us. We will post the time and title of the talk once the schedule is published.

Until then, the Exchange documentation has everything needed to try it, and we would love to hear how your Outlook clients get on with Stalwart.
